paragraphs.text: Again, by the hope of God, we write a treatise on the soul, composed as far as he was able by the holy Mar Moses the bishop, who is surnamed Bar Kepha.

"Soul," then, is a word with several meanings, and it is used in many senses in Scripture and in nature and common usage. We speak of the nature of God as "soul," as the Lord said through Isaiah the prophet: "Your feasts and your new moons my soul hates"; and as in: "The Lord of hosts has sworn by his soul." This is not because God has a human soul (God forbid!). Here divine Scripture gives the name "soul" to the nature and being of God. The whole human being, who is made up of soul and body, is also called a soul, as it is written in Ezekiel the prophet: "The soul that sins, it shall die." Here Scripture calls the whole composite a soul, and we know this because death is the dissolution of the composite. The body alone is also called a soul, when names and sufferings are transferred from death to the dead [?] because the parts are united with one another. So it is written in David concerning Joseph: "His soul entered into iron." Blood is also called a soul, as Moses said: "The soul of all flesh is blood." Here he gives the name "soul" to the blood alone. The nourishing and growth-producing power that trees, grass, seeds and everything that is nourished and grows possess is also called a soul. The philosophers call it "ensouled" and "animating," and this power is called the vegetative soul. The power of sensation and motion that all animals possess is also called a soul, and this power is called the animal and elemental soul. It is called animal because the wise men of the Church, and the outside philosophers as well, call "animal" everything that perceives, moves from place to place and lives. It is called elemental because it is composed out of the composition of the elements. All irrational animals have this animal and elemental soul, and so do human bodies. Finally, the rational soul that is in us is also called soul. By it we receive the law; it distinguishes good from evil and truth from falsehood, and it governs the body and enables it to move rationally. So "soul" is used in seven senses in divine Scripture, in other writings and in common usage. The table set out below shows these seven more clearly. 1: The being and nature of God, as in: "Your feasts and your new moons my soul hates." 2: The whole human being, as in: "The soul that sins, it shall die." 3: The body alone: "A soul that is sated tramples honeycombs." 4: The blood alone: "The soul of all flesh is blood." 5: Vegetative: (the nourishing and growth-producing power that trees and grass possess). 6: Animal: the power of sensation and motion that [?] animals and bodies. 7: Rational: [?] we distinguish good from evil and move rationally. In this book, however, our concern is with the rational soul, not with these others.

A demonstration that the soul exists. Here someone asks: "How do we know that the soul exists, when none of the senses perceives it? It is not seen with the eyes, nor heard with the ears, nor tasted with the palate, nor touched with the hand, nor smelled with the nostrils. How, then, is it known that the soul exists?" First, we know that the soul exists from its name. A name signifies something, and "soul" is a name. Therefore the name "soul" signifies something. But someone may object that "non-existent" is also a name, and so it too signifies something. We reply that "non-existent" is not a name, but a name only in a certain sense, and that which was added to it [?] … is not a name [?]. He may object again that there is a name [?] … for something, such as "goat-stag," which is a name [?] … that signifies something, in that [?] … a thing composed of a goat and a stag. We reply again that [?] … "goat-stag" [?] … does not signify a nature composed of a goat and a stag, since no such thing exists. It signifies simple thoughts put together, made up of goat and stag, for as Aristotle says, names signify thoughts. So it has been shown that a name signifies something, and "soul" is a name. Therefore the name "soul" signifies something, and so it has been made plain that the soul exists.

We also know that the soul exists because we see the body moving at one time and ceasing from its motion at another. While it is alive it moves, but when it is dead it ceases from its motion. Its motion comes either from itself or from some other nature. If it came from itself, it would never cease from its motion. It is clear, therefore, that something else moves it, and that is the soul. If someone objects [?] … that the body's motion comes from its elements, we reply that in that case it ought not to cease from its motion until its elements are dissolved from one another and its parts are separated and scattered, (if these are) the cause of its motion, as you say. But we see it cease from its motion while its elements are not yet dissolved and scattered, so it is clear that its motion comes from something else, which is the soul. Again someone may object: "Look, we see that irrational animals also move at one time and not at another. While alive they move, and when dead they cease from motion. Then they too must have a rational soul that moves their bodies." We reply that these are not moved by a rational soul, as human bodies are, but by some other cause. We will show this, God willing, as we already showed in the first chapter, where we said that the soul of irrational animals is the power of sensation and motion. This power is the cause of the motion of their bodies and is called the animal soul. If he objects yet again and says that this animal soul also moves human bodies, we reply that the rational soul moves human bodies, while the animal soul moves the bodies of irrational animals. We know this because the rational soul enables human beings to move rationally, while the animal soul enables animals to move irrationally. Rational motion differs from irrational motion in many respects, for a human being differs in that he eats, drinks and mates rationally.

Everything that moves is moved either from within or from without. What is moved from without is like a millstone, which is turned by a mule or by water. What is moved from within is like fire, which moves by its own nature and being. What is moved from without ceases from its motion from time to time, but what is moved from within does not cease. The body is not moved from without. We know this because it is not dragged or pulled like soulless objects, which are dragged and pulled when something outside them moves them. It remains, then, that the body is moved from within. Yet although it is moved from within, it does not move by its own nature, as fire does, but by something else. We know that fire moves naturally because it never ceases from its motion as long as it is fire. The body, however, does not move naturally, as we know from the fact that it ceases from its motion while it is still a body. So the body is not moved from without, like soulless objects, nor naturally, like fire. It remains that it is moved by the soul, which is also the cause of its life.

We are like stones and iron in having bodies, but we differ from them in having sensation. We are also like the animals in moving from place to place, in living, in seeing, in hearing and in the rest of the senses, and [?] like them we grow angry and feel desire. In what, then, do we differ from them? Clearly in the rational soul. Therefore the soul exists.

Either the whole human being is mortal and corruptible, or the whole is immortal and incorruptible, or part of him is mortal and corruptible and part immortal and incorruptible. Or else we should call the soul the human being, as [?] Plato [says]; or the whole human being is mortal and corruptible; or we should call the body alone the human being, as the Stoics say; or part of the human being is mortal and corruptible, as Pilatus [?] says, and this is the true view. It is known, then, that the soul exists from the fact [?] … that part of the human being is mortal and corruptible, namely the body, while part is immortal and incorruptible, namely the soul.

The wise agree that there are substances and there are accidents, and that some of these, whether substances or accidents, are perceived by the senses and others by the intellect. Accidents must subsist in substances, since they have no existence apart from substances. It is also agreed that there are blackness, whiteness and the rest, as well as good and evil, righteousness and wickedness. Whiteness, blackness and corporeal qualities subsist simply (in a body), while sickness and health subsist in a body that has a soul. But in what do good and evil, righteousness and wickedness subsist? Clearly in the soul. Whiteness and blackness are sensible accidents, and they subsist in a body, which is a sensible substance. So righteousness and wickedness, which are intelligible accidents, must subsist in an intelligible substance. Therefore the soul exists.

We also know that the soul exists from its activity. Often a person closes the eyes of his body and sees with other eyes within. He keeps his mouth silent and speaks in his heart, blessing whomever he wishes and cursing whomever he wishes. While he is on earth he sees the things in heaven as he meditates. While he is in one place nearby, he gazes at distant places and sees what is there, though his body does not move. And there are times when his tongue is silent, yet he brings the thought of his heart into the open and makes it known to others in writing. Again, we see a physician lay his hand on the body of a sick person in plain view, feel it, and discover hidden pains and ailments. All these activities, and others like them, belong not to the body but to the soul.

We also know that the soul exists from the inventions of the arts. Where else do smithing, architecture, carpentry, weaving, geometry, astronomy, arithmetic, music and all the other arts come from, if not from the rational soul? Someone may object that irrational animals also have arts: the bee has the work of the honeycomb, the spider [?] its wonderful weaving, and the ant its gathering of grain. We give him two answers. First, irrational animals do these things by nature, compelled by the necessity of nature, and not voluntarily from a rational soul. Human beings, by contrast, learn arts voluntarily from a rational soul, and not because the necessity of nature compels them. Second, irrational animals need no teachers or instruction to practise an art, but human beings need masters and pupils. All these arts are inventions of the rational soul.

We also know that the soul exists from the forethought that it has, and from the fact that it carries out its work through the body, which is its instrument, and impresses that work on matter. Often a carpenter first pictures in his mind the chair he wants to make. He forms its shape, its height, depth and breadth, its beauty, its usefulness and everything else. Afterwards he brings out with his hands, with adze, wood and movement, the work that he had first fashioned in his will. So too the architect when he wants to build a house, and the smith when he wants [?] an iron nail. This forethought belongs to the rational soul. Therefore the soul exists.

We also know that the soul exists from two opposing activities found in a human being. Often a person is hungry yet does not eat, thirsty yet does not drink, and wishes to mate yet does not mate. All these are activities of the body. What is this desire by which the body desires to eat and drink, yet does not eat or drink, unless there is another nature that restrains it? And what causes the body to desire sleep or mating, yet not sleep or mate, unless there is another nature that holds it back? This is not found in irrational animals. When an ass is hungry and finds straw or barley, it cannot keep from eating. When it desires to mate and finds an opportunity, it cannot keep from mating. It has no rational soul to hold it back from its irrational passions, so that it might be hungry, find food and not feed, or be thirsty, find drink and not drink. It is the body that desires, but what holds it back from its desire is not the body. It is the body that wants to eat, but what makes it fast against its desire is not the body. It is the body that wants to mate, but what restrains it is not the body. The body flees from blows and from death, but what hands it over to death and blows in the hope of something is not the body. This is something [?], which is the soul. So too a human being, because he has a rational soul, is able both to act and not to act. Often, while his eyes are looking, he closes them so as not to see, and while his ears are hearing, he stops them so as not to hear. But irrational animals cannot choose not to see or to see, to hear or not to hear. So it has been made plain that the soul exists. If, then, a human being has two opposing activities, one that sustains the body and another that destroys it, it is clear that this…

…an activity that runs counter to that of the body belongs to the soul. But if someone objects and says that these two opposing activities come from the elements, we answer him that the elements of which man is composed do not oppose one another in the urge of desire in the way that the activity of the soul opposes the activity of the body. For there are times when the body wants to eat and the soul does not allow it to eat, for whatever reason it wishes. We see that the irrational animals are driven by man, and serve and are made subject to him. And although they are quite equal to man in everything that comes from the elements, there is not a single kind of animal that is subject to its fellow, serves it and supplies its needs, as they are subject to man and supply his need. Clearly this is because there is in him another nature, stronger than his elements, namely the soul; and on account of this the animals are subject to him and do service for him. It is also clear that there is a soul in man from the fact that he constructs syllogisms and distinguishes truth from falsehood and good from evil. It is clear that there is a soul from

the definition of man, that he is a living, rational, mortal being. "Living" and "rational" are said on account of the soul, and "mortal" on account of the body. Each of these members, through which the senses of the body operate, has a single activity: the eyes to see, the ears to hear, the mouth to taste, the nostrils to smell, the hands to touch. But which of the things the eyes see and the ears hear is useful and which is not useful, and which of the things the hands touch is good and beneficial and which is harmful — this activity is not a sense, that the senses should examine and distinguish it, nor does it belong to the body; it belongs to the rational soul, which distinguishes what is ours from what is not ours, and what is useful from what is not useful ……… Here there are six lines which have been effaced and cannot be read. … bodily things: hot … and cold from soft [?], and salty from insipid, and so on. But spiritual things, when they are higher than it [?]. I mean those that help and are useful and those that do not; those that are good and beneficial, and those

that are not: it is the rational soul that distinguishes them, and not the body. If again he objects and says that this discernment is the temperament of the body, we answer him: then this discernment ought to be found more in elephants and camels than in small animals. Yet we see that the tiny ones are more cunning, such as the fox. It is clear that man has a soul from the fact that laws are laid down for him, that he should do these things and not do those, which cannot happen with the irrational animals. No one lays down a law for [?] not to steal, or for doves not to commit adultery, or for [?] to keep chastity, or for sheep to be simple and meek, or for donkeys to fast and pray. But man, because he has a rational soul …………. It is clear that man has a soul from the fact that he fears Gehenna ……… the kingdom, and does good …… hoping, as he looks to the reward …… well; these belong to the rational soul, which distinguishes them and carries them out. So much for the natural and rational proofs. We show that there is a soul from the holy Scriptures as well. Moses said that the Lord God formed

Adam from the ground and breathed into his face the breath of life, and Adam became a living soul. David sang: "Bless the Lord, O my soul"; and, "His spirit goes forth, and he returns to his earth"; and, "My soul shall rejoice in God"; and, "Praise the Lord, O my soul." Solomon said that the body returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit to the Lord who gave it; and again, "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God." Zechariah said that he created the spirit of man within him. Elijah said: "O Lord God, let the soul of this child return into him." Hananiah and his companions said: "Bless the Lord, you souls and spirits of the righteous." Ezekiel said: "Come, O spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon the slain, that they may live." The Lord said: "What will a man gain if he acquires the whole world and loses his soul?" and, "They cannot kill the soul." Stephen said: "And they were seventy-five souls in number." Peter said: "And now you have turned to the shepherd of your souls." John again said: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves." Paul said: "For not one soul among you will be lost"; and again, "Let us cleanse ourselves from filth in the holiness of the Spirit." Which shows the opinions and thoughts

of the outside teachers concerning the soul. Now the outside philosophers: some of them held and said that the soul is a body, others that it is incorporeal. Of those who called it a body, some said it is a single element, others that it is composed of many elements. Of those who said it is from a single element, some said it is from water — this was Thales; others said air — this was Anaximenes; others called it fire — this was Heraclitus. But none of them dared to say that the soul is from earth, because of the great opposition between the subtlety of the soul and the nature of earth. Of those who said it is composed of many elements, some said it is the blood surrounding the heart — this was Empedocles; others called it breath — this was Hippocrates; others a compound of tiny bodies that fly in the air — this was Democritus. All these, then, who said that the soul is a body were Stoics, who said that everything is body, and who called even God himself a subtle body.

Those who said that the soul is incorporeal are also divided. Some of them said that it is a substance, subsisting of and by itself, and that it has no need to subsist in another; others said that it is not a substance, not subsisting of and by itself but in another. Those who called it a substance subsisting of and by itself said that it has a nature of its own, which moves and lives and has activity of and by itself. Of those who said that it is not a substance but subsists in another, some said that it is like sight in the eye, whiteness in snow and sweetness in hon[ey] … others said that it is the power of the mixture of the elements … [?] for an activity born of their combination, which was not found in any one of them of and by itself. Just as when honey, wine and pepper are combined together, an effect is born from them which none of them had before; and as when many roots are combined and kneaded together, a potency is born from them which was not in any one of them before they were kneaded together; so also the elements, when they are mixed in equal measure, a body is formed from them, and from their mixture is born that power which was not in any one of them

before. This power is the nature of the soul. And just as an activity, an effect or a power perishes when separated from the things in which it subsists, so too the soul perishes when it is separated from the body. This, then, was the opinion of Alexander of Aphrodisias. Others said that the soul is the harmony of the combination of the elements, taking this from the likeness of the harmony that is formed in ordered sound from the strings of a lyre; and just as the [harmony of the lyre] … when the strings of the lyre are separated from it …, so too the soul after it is separated from the body. This was the opinion of Hippocrates. Others said that it is the entelechy of the body, that is, its completion, this form of the body. This was Aristotle. It is right, then, to examine this. Aristotle said that there are three substances: one of them is matter, which is the substrate; another is the form and species by which matter is moved; and another is that which is composed of these two — of matter, I mean, and of form. The substance which is matter he calls potentiality, because it is able

to receive form. The substance which is form and species he calls entelechy, because it is the completion of the body. To give a clear illustration of what Aristotle says: take, for matter, the likeness of pure, plain bronze that has not yet received any shape at all; for form and likeness, the shape of a statue; and for substance, the statue, which is composed of bronze and shape. Aristotle therefore recognized it in three ways: (1) one, from matter, he calls potentiality, like unshaped and unworked bronze; (2) another, the form and likeness, he calls entelechy, like the likeness, shape and form; (3) and another, that which is composed of matter and form, as a statue is composed of bronze and the shape of a man. Aristotle therefore said that the soul is entelechy in this sense: that it is the completion and form of the body, just as the shape and form of a statue are the shaping and completion of the statue,

when the bronze has passed from what it was in potentiality into actuality, since it is the substance of the statue. So too the soul is the completion and form of the body, and therefore it is the entelechy of the body. And again, just as sight completes the eye, so the soul completes the living being. These are some of the opinions and thoughts which the outside philosophers held and thought about the soul. They become known more clearly from this division set out below: Some said that the soul is a body: some of them said that it is a single element, others many elements. Some called it fire: Heraclitus. Others said air: Anaximenes. Others said it is from water: Empedocles. Others called it breath that blows: Hippocrates. Others a compound of tiny bodies that fly in the air: Democritus. Of those who held it incorporeal, some said that it subsists of and by itself in its own subsistence; others the harmony of the combination of the elements: Anacrates; others called it the entelechy of the body: Aristotle; others the power of the equal mixture of the elements: Alexander of Aphrodisias; others that it does not subsist of and by itself (some said like sight in the eye) but in another.

There are others who held other views which do not fit into this division and are not included under it. Asclepiades said that the soul is the exercise of the senses. Pythagoras said that the soul is a number that moves itself. Others said that the soul is a collection of understanding and memory: just as a sheet of paper or an unwritten scroll is receptive of writing and of understanding, because things are written and imprinted on it, so too the human body, when it is formed, has in it no thought, no understanding and no memory [?]; but afterwards, through the experiences that befall it one by one, a collection of thoughts and understanding is formed in it, and this memory, they say, is the soul. Plato, again, said that even in irrational animals there is a rational soul. The Manichaeans, again, held these three opinions about the soul: first, that the soul is incorporeal; second, that it is immortal; third, that the soul is one, is not divided, and is in each and every body; animate things share in a great deal of it, inanimate things in a little, and the heavenly bodies share in it abundantly and greatly. A counter-argument

against these opinions of the philosophers that have been stated, and a refutation of the claims that they vaunted as true concerning the soul. First we answer all those Stoics who maintain that the soul is a body. The Stoics put forward three arguments by which they show that the soul is a body. Their first argument: they say that we resemble our parents not only in body but also in soul, in passions, habits and disposition. Resemblance belongs to bodies, not to what is incorporeal. Therefore the soul is a body. We resolve their first argument thus: resemblance and unlikeness belong to quality, and quality is incorporeal; for the incorporeal is like and unlike the incorporeal. The second argument: no incorporeal thing suffers together with a body when it is pained or cut; but the body suffers together with the soul when it suffers likewise: when the soul is ashamed, the body turns red, and when it is afraid, it turns pale. Therefore the soul is a body, because it suffers together with the body. Resolution: first we answer their first point that there are some incorporeal things that suffer together with a body, as qualities do;

for though they are incorporeal, they suffer together with bodies: they too become alike with them, and when bodies are heated, they are heated along with them. Then we answer their second point thus: when the body suffers from the soul, it receives from it the sensation by which it feels, while the soul remains impassible and, without suffering, benefits it. The third argument: death is the separation of the soul from the body. No incorporeal thing is separated from a body, nor is it even joined to a body. But the soul is both joined to the body and separated from it. Therefore the soul is a body. Resolution: what you said, that death is the separation of the soul from the body, is true. But when you said that the incorporeal is neither joined to a body nor separated from it, that is false, since a mark and whiteness, which are incorporeal, are joined to a body and separated from it. Again, we say that the soul is not joined to the body by contact. For if it were joined to it by contact, it would be placed beside it or alongside it. Again, if it were joined to it by contact, the whole of it would not be ensouled, nor would the whole of it live, but

only a part of it, the part that was in contact with the soul, would be ensouled and living. But if the whole of it is ensouled and lives, the soul is united to the whole of it and bound with the whole of it, and not joined to it by contact. These, then, are the three arguments of the Stoics and our resolution of them. The demonstrations by which we show that the soul is not a body are these: 1. Every body whatever falls under one of the senses, or under all of them, and is therefore perceptible. But the soul is not perceptible: it is neither seen nor touched, and so on. Therefore it is not a body. 2. A body added to another body adds weight to it. But the soul is in the body, and not only does it add no weight to it, it gives it life and makes it light. Therefore it is not a body. 3. A body does not pass through a body, because the one hinders the other and the parts of each are impeded by the other. But the soul passes through the whole of it and dwells there. Therefore it is not a body. 4. Every body that moves is moved either from outside, like a millstone that is pushed from outside, or from inside, like an animate body. Now the soul is not moved from outside

like an inanimate body. Therefore it is not a body. And if someone says that the soul is moved from inside like an animate body, that is false and absurd. 5. The accidents of a body are bodily, like whiteness and blackness, which subsist in a body. But the accidents of the soul are incorporeal, like love, hatred, distress and joy. Therefore it is not a body, if bodies subsist in what is incorporeal. 6. An animate body is nourished by bodily food; but the soul is not nourished by bodily food. Therefore it is not a body. 7. An animate body grows and increases in length, depth and breadth; but the soul does not grow in these. Therefore it is not a body. 8. Every body whatever is in a place, which contains it, and two bodies cannot be in one place. But body and soul are in one place. Therefore the soul is not a body. 9. There is no body that is rational and knowing by its nature; but the soul is by nature rationality and knowledge. Therefore it is not a body. 10. Every

body whatever is united to another body through the contact of its surfaces. But the soul is united whole with whole, without contact. Therefore it is not a body. So much against those who say that the soul is a body. Against those who say that the soul is water or air. These say that it is clear the soul is water or air from the fact that one cannot live without water and air. We say two things to them. First, that one cannot live without food and nourishment either; then let these also be the soul, by your reasoning. Second, that there are many animals that live without drinking water, as they say of eagles and partridges; and there are many others that live without breathing air, such as insects — bees and wasps, for instance — and those that have no lungs, I mean fish, eels and so on. Therefore the soul is neither air nor water. Against those who say that the soul is fire. We have already shown many times that the soul is incorporeal, and so we show by the following that the soul is not fire: 1. Fire is a body; but the soul is not a body. Therefore the soul is not

fire. 2. Fire is perceptible; but the soul is not perceptible. Therefore the soul is not fire. 3. Fire, whenever it is active in a body, sets it ablaze and burns it up [?]. Therefore the soul is not fire. Against those who say that the soul is blood and breath. They say that it is clear the soul is blood and breath from the fact that when blood and breath are separated from a living creature, the creature dies. We answer them: if you call these the soul because the creature dies when they are separated from it, then the head, the brain, the heart and the liver are also the soul, since when any one of them, or all of them, is separated from the creature, the creature dies. And again, if it is as you say, then a portion of blood that flows out is a portion of the soul flowing out — and this is absurd and false. Against those who say that the soul is a compound of elements, or of tiny bodies that fly in the air. 1. A compound of tiny bodies is bodies; but the soul is incorporeal. Therefore the soul is not a compound of tiny bodies. 2. A compound of tiny bodies is perceptible; but the soul is not perceptible. Therefore the soul is not

a compound of tiny bodies. [3.] A compound of tiny bodies is composite; but the soul is simple. Therefore the soul is not a compound of tiny flying bodies. Against those who say that the soul is incorporeal, not subsisting of and by itself but subsisting in another. We shall speak against them in general, God willing, in what follows, where we show that the soul is a substance … and after it is separated from the body it subsists of and by itself, with a subsistence of its own. Here, however, we speak specifically to each of them. First, against those who say that the soul is like sight in the eyes and whiteness in snow. 1. Sight and whiteness in snow are accidents; but the soul is a substance, as we shall show, God willing. Therefore the soul is not like sight in the eyes and whiteness in snow. 2. Sight in the eyes and the whiteness in snow belong to the things that are in a substrate; but the soul is itself a substrate, and not one of the things that are in it, for it is the substrate of righteousness and wickedness, of knowledge and ignorance. Therefore the soul is not like sight in the eyes

and like whiteness in snow. Against those who say that the soul is the power of the equal mixture of the elements. 1. The power of the equal mixture of the elements is a quality; but the soul is a substance, as we shall show, God willing. Therefore the soul is not the power of the equal mixture of the elements. 2. The power of the mixture is perceptible; but the soul is intelligible. Therefore the soul is not the power of the mixture. 3. The power of the equal mixture of the elements makes the body healthy. If, then, the soul is the power of the equal mixture of the elements, a man ought not to fall sick or grow weak as long as he lives and has a soul in him. Yet we see that he falls sick and grows weak while he lives and has a soul in him. 4. The equal powers of the mixture of the elements depart from the body, yet the soul remains in it. Therefore the soul is not the power of the equal mixture of the elements. If the soul is the power of the equal mixture of the elements — 5. the power of the mixture of the elements changes with ages, ways of life and time; then the soul too would change

and would not remain one and the same for us, but would be now one thing and now another, according to the power of the mixture of the elements, which changes: at one time that of a lion, at another that of a lamb, at another that of a wolf, at another that of a kid. But if this is false and absurd, the soul is not the power of the equal mixture of the elements. 6. If the soul is the power of the equal mixture of the elements, every body made of the elements that has the power of the mixture has a soul. Then every body has a soul. And if every body has a soul, then stones and iron have a soul, and inanimate things turn out to be animate — which is false and absurd. Therefore the soul is not the equal power of the elements. Against those who say that the soul is the harmony of the combination of the elements, calling harmony an attunement. 1. The soul often opposes the body, restraining it from its desire or handing it over to those who chastise it. But harmony, that is, the attunement of the elements, does not oppose the body; and if it opposes it, it is not an attunement. Therefore the soul is not

the harmony of the combination of the elements. 2. The soul has precedence and headship over the body; but the attunement of the elements has no precedence or headship over the body. Therefore the soul is not an attunement. 3. The soul receives righteousness and wickedness, chastity and excellence; but the attunement of the elements receives none of these. Therefore the soul is not an attunement. 4. The soul is a substance, as we shall show, God willing; but attunement is a quality. Therefore the soul is not the attunement of the elements. 5. If the soul is the harmony, that is, the attunement, of the elements — and attunement is the health of the body — then a man ought not to fall sick or grow weak as long as he lives and has a soul in him. For the attunement of the elements departs from the body, while the soul is preserved in it even when he is sick. Therefore the soul is not the harmony, that is, the attunement, of the combination of the elements. Against those who say that Aristotle said the soul is the entelechy of the body. First we say that entelechy is completion, and that the entelechy of a thing is spoken of in two senses. One is that which is not the governor

of a thing, and when it is separated from it, does not endure — like the shape of a ship, which is the entelechy, or completion, of the ship, and like the shape of a man, which is the entelechy of a statue. This entelechy, when separated from that to which it belongs, does not endure. The other kind of entelechy is that which is the governor of a thing and which, when separated from it, endures — like the sailor, who is the entelechy, or completion, of the ship and also its governor. This entelechy, when separated from that to which it belongs, endures and subsists of and by itself. So there are two: 1. one, which is the governor of a thing, endures when separated from it; 2. the other is not the governor of a thing, and when separated from it does not endure. If, then, Aristotle said that the soul is the entelechy of the body in the way that the sailor is the entelechy, or completion, of the ship — in that it is the one that fits the body together and governs it — he spoke well. For he is said to have

a book in which he calls the soul a rational being. But if he said that the soul is the entelechy of the body in the way that the shape of a ship is its entelechy and the shape of a statue is the entelechy of the statue, he spoke badly and very foolishly. And if that is what he said of the soul, we put these refutations to him: 1. If the soul is the entelechy of the body in the way that the shape of a statue is by nature, then necessarily, when the hand of a living man is cut off, a part of the soul would be cut off with it, as a part of the bronze and a part of the shape are. But it is evident that the soul cannot be cut, as we shall show, God willing. Therefore the soul is not the entelechy of the body in the way that shape is the entelechy of a statue. 2. If the soul were the entelechy of the body like the shape of a ship, it could not fight against the body. Yet we see it standing against its passions in many things and many times: a man longs to eat or drink or have intercourse, and the soul sometimes restrains him from it. Therefore the soul is not the entelechy of the body. 3. If the soul were the entelechy of the body like the shape of the body of a ship, it could not hold within it the impressions, images and likenesses

of bodies when they are far from it, after it has seen them. Yet we see that it receives them and they are preserved in it. 4. If the soul is the entelechy of the body, then it receives its existence from the body, and the body is superior to it, since it is the cause of its coming to be; and hence the soul is inferior to that from which it came to be. But it is clear and evident that the soul is superior to the body in many things, and that it has filled the world with knowledge, wisdom, crafts and so on. Therefore the soul is not the entelechy of the body in the way that shape is the entelechy of a ship or a house. Against those who say that the soul is the exercise of the senses, a number that moves itself, or a collection of understanding and memory. (1) The exercise of the senses, understanding and memory are accidents; but the soul is a substance. Therefore the soul is not the exercise of the senses, number, understanding or memory. (2) For these are among the things that are in a substrate, whereas the soul is the substrate. Therefore the soul is not exercise, number, understanding or memory. (3) Moreover, the exercise of the senses, understanding, memory and number do not move the body rationally. Therefore the soul is not

the exercise of the senses, number, understanding or memory. Against Plato, who said that even in irrational animals there is a soul. We say that there is a soul in irrational animals, and it is clear from these demonstrations: First: there is in irrational animals not a single rational movement — neither understanding, nor reasoning, nor letters, nor crafts, which are the discoveries of the rational soul. 2. It is clear that there is no rational soul in them from the fact that they cannot receive a law, which is the mark of the rational soul. No one has ever laid down a law for doves, or a donkey, or a fish, that they should fast or pray. 3. It is clear that there are no rational souls in them from the fact that they do not obtain any of the delight of the world to come, nor do they look to the reward that is to come, or to what has been promised. 4. It is clear that they have no rational soul from the fact that no opposing activities are seen in them. I mean that, when they are hungry and have food, they cannot refrain from eating; and when they long for mating and find the opportunity, they cannot hold back, but at once they mate,

and likewise with other things. 5. It is clear, again, that there is no rational soul in irrational animals from the fact that each of them performs one and the same activity, that of its kind, even if it performs it to a greater degree, and it cannot change that activity or fail to perform it in the same way. Camels, for example, are all vengeful; wolves rapacious; lions bold; hares timid; foxes cunning; peacocks proud. From this it is clear that they are moved not rationally but irrationally. 6. And if one of the Platonists objects and says that children too are not moved rationally, we answer him: even if at the age of childhood they do not display rational activity, yet at the age that follows they act rationally. But irrational animals display no rational activities at any age, only irrational ones. And if they object again and say that these are rational activities, and that rational movement is found in them, but that the formation of their members is not able to receive rational activity

like people who have lost their fingers and are idle from a craft. We say to them: according to what they say, then, the Creator did not make for them a soul suited to their bodies, but one unsuited to them. If this is so, God created the souls of irrational animals in vain. But it is false that God created anything in vain. As one of the wise said about created things and becoming: he did not create a single one of them idly. If not even one wise human being does anything in vain, how much less God.

Against the Manichaeans, who say that the soul is incorporeal, that it is divided among each one of the bodies, and that it is immortal. If it really is divided, it is not incorporeal but a body. The incorporeal does not admit division into parts at all, whereas a body is certainly divided. By this you have falsified your own statement that the soul is incorporeal. If the soul really is divided, it is a body; and if it is a body, it is mortal, for everything that lives and is a body is mortal.

So you have also undone that other statement of yours which says that the soul is immortal. And if the soul is one, as you have said, and really is divided among each one of the bodies, then stones and iron, which are inanimate bodies, would turn out to be ensouled and not inanimate, which is false. Therefore the soul is not as the Manichaeans suppose.

Showing that the soul is a substance. That the soul is a substance is known from these proofs. 1. This, then, is the property of substance, as the wise reason: that while remaining one and the same it receives contraries through its own change, so to speak. A body is a substance; at one time it becomes white, at another black. And the living body, being a substance, is at one time healthy and at another sick. Thus body and living body, which are substances, receive whiteness and blackness, health and sickness, which are contrary accidents. In the same way the soul too, while it is one and the same, at one time receives righteousness and becomes

righteous, and at another receives wickedness and becomes wicked. In the same way it also receives chastity and wantonness from time to time, which are contrary to each other. If, then, this is the property of substance, that while changing in its nature it receives contraries in turn, then the soul is a substance. 2. That the soul is a substance is known from the body, which is a substance. For it is impossible that what is moved, acted upon and governed should be a substance [?]. Since, then, the body, which is moved, is a substance, the soul, which moves it, must necessarily be a substance as well. 3. That it is a substance is known from the learning that we acquire: it does not subsist in our body. This is known from the fact that not everything that is a body receives learning. For behold, irrational animals are corporeal, yet they do not receive learning and knowledge. The soul, however, does receive learning, and learning subsists in it as accidents subsist in a substance. 4. That it is a substance is known from the fact that it is preserved and endures after its release from the body, as we shall show, God willing.

Showing that the soul is incorporeal. That the soul is incorporeal, then, is known from these syllogisms, which are constructed in the first figure. 1. A body has three dimensions: length, depth and breadth. But the soul does not have three dimensions. Therefore it is incorporeal. 2. Every body is perceptible to the senses. But the five senses do not apprehend the soul. Therefore it is incorporeal. 3. When a body is added to another body and attached to it, it adds weight to it. But the soul adds no weight to the body when it is united with it. Therefore it is [? incorporeal]. 4. Incorporeal accidents befall the soul, such as righteousness and wickedness, virtue and vice. But incorporeal accidents do not befall a body. Therefore the soul is not a body. 5. The soul is nourished by incorporeal food, by learning, I mean, and by knowledge. But a body is not nourished by incorporeal food. Therefore the soul is not

a body. Moreover, one body cannot be together with another body in one place and one position while they are united. Therefore the soul is not a body. 6. The soul possesses knowledge from its own nature. But a body does not possess knowledge and perception from its own nature. Therefore the soul is incorporeal. Other proofs showing that the soul is incorporeal are in the fourth chapter. These, then, are from the syllogisms that show that the soul is incorporeal.

The testimonies from the holy Scriptures that confirm that the soul is incorporeal are these. Our Lord says in his Gospel: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." This shows, first, that the soul is incorporeal, and second, that it is immortal because it is incorporeal: incorporeal, in that it cannot receive the sword or the sufferings that befall the body, which is a body; and immortal, in that it is not killed as the body is killed. Again he says: "Not by bread

alone shall a man live, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God." By saying "but by every word," he showed that the soul is nourished by words; and by its being nourished by words and teachings he showed that it is incorporeal. Again the apostle Paul says this about himself: "I know a man in Christ — whether in the body or without the body I do not know; God knows — who was caught up to the third heaven." Now by saying "or without the body," he showed that the nature of the soul is neither bodily nor corporeal, but is another, incorporeal nature, distinct from the nature of the body. Again he wrote to the Hebrews: "Remember those who are afflicted, as people who are yourselves clothed in flesh." He showed that the garment is other than the one who is clothed in it: the garment is a body. It is clear, then, that the soul, which is clothed with the flesh, is incorporeal. And again the prophet David says: "Let us hear what the Lord our God will speak." And many times the prophet [?] God as he spoke. And just as

his speech [?] came forth from a bodily mouth, so too the prophets did not hear him with bodily ears, but with [? incorporeal] souls. Therefore it has been shown by what has been said that the soul is incorporeal.

Showing that the soul is simple. The soul is simple, and this is known from these arguments. The soul is incorporeal, and everything incorporeal is simple; therefore the soul is simple. The soul is not divided or cut into parts, and everything that is not divided into parts is simple; therefore the soul is simple. The soul is not composed of elements, and everything that is not composed of elements is simple; therefore the soul is simple. These come from three syllogisms in the first figure on the soul's being simple.

Showing what we ought to investigate first: the nature of the soul, its power, or its activity. We say that there are these three: nature, powers and activity. Nature is something that subsists; the powers subsist in the nature; and activities come from the powers. Whoever investigates the powers or the activity while neglecting first to investigate the nature is like a blind man who, from hearsay alone, wants to compound drugs and paint beautiful pictures and handsome likenesses. We ought first to investigate the nature of the soul, what it is, because it is the first thing on which the discerning mind settles, since it subsists of itself and for itself and never subsists in another, because it is and is called a substance; and further, because the powers too have their subsistence in the nature itself. After that we should investigate the power of the soul, because the powers precede activity. Then we investigate the activities of the soul, because they come from the powers. Therefore we ought first to investigate the nature of the soul.

Showing what the nature of the soul is. Someone may rightly ask: what is the nature of the soul? We say that the nature of the soul is life. If he objects and says, "How is it known that its nature is life?", we say that it is known from these proofs. 1. Everything that lives by its own nature, and not through another, is alive by nature. The soul lives by its own nature and not through another. Therefore its nature is life. 2. The body is not alive by its own nature but lives through another. This is known from the fact that when the life that is in it departs, it remains lifeless. But the soul's nature is life, and this is known from the fact that its nature never remains while being lifeless. 3. That whose nature is life does not come to an end; and the soul does not come to an end; therefore its nature is life. And that whose nature is life does not die; and the soul does not die; therefore its nature is life. It has been shown clearly by these arguments that the nature of the soul is life. But if someone objects and says, "If that is so, the nature of the angel is also life; and so the nature of the soul [?]

would be the very nature of the angel, and the nature of the angel would be that of the soul," we say to him: it is not because the nature of the soul is equal to the nature of the angel in being life that the nature of the angel and that of the soul must be one. For although the nature of the soul is life, life differs from life, in that the life of the angel is higher and more exalted than that of the soul. And just as life is higher than life, so too one nature is higher and more exalted than another. Again, although the nature of angels is life, they are not united with bodies; and by this the life of angels surpasses that of the soul, and so too does their nature. Again, the soul has properties by which its nature is distinguished from that of the angel. Therefore it has been shown by these arguments that the nature of the soul is life. Again we say that the nature of the soul is immortal. And when we speak of the immortality of the soul, we do not signify a privation but a possession, as we shall show, God willing. And what possession do we signify when we speak of the immortality of

the soul? We say: life. So it is the same thing to say "life" of the soul as to signify its nature, for its nature is life. And when we say that the nature of the soul is immortality, we signify that it is life. Likewise, when immortality is spoken of angels, it signifies life and not privation. Therefore the nature of the soul is life. Gregory bears witness to this, saying thus in the oration on the Nativity: "From matter he took the body, and from himself he placed in it life, which the Word knows as the intelligent soul and the image of God."

Showing the powers and activities of the soul. Of the powers of the soul, some are natural and some are accidental. The natural ones are: intellect, understanding, cognition, rationality, motion, memory, and those like these. The accidental ones are: anger, desire, perception through the five senses, imagination, and those like these.

1. Of the powers of the soul, some are natural: intellect, understanding, cognition, rationality, self-motion, memory. 2. Of the powers of the soul, some are accidental: anger, desire, perception through the five senses, imagination. These are the powers of the soul, together with those like them. But powers are not known except through their activities, because they are hidden, and what is hidden is known through its activity. Therefore we ought to explain these powers and make them known from their activities. We define them thus. Intellect is the power that knows things not through words, nor through demonstrations, nor even through teaching, but through that

hidden and simple vision that the saints have in the life of souls. Understanding is that which knows things through words, demonstrations, teachings and syllogisms. Cognition is a power …… [?] is the activity that distinguishes true thoughts from false ones. This, then, is how philosophers define rationality: as the power that discerns thoughts. Self-motion is a power that is moved by itself and not by anything else. Memory is the power that gathers and preserves the knowledge of what has been learned, in that it gathers it and keeps it so that it is not lost. These are the activities that come from the natural powers of the soul, and they define them. The activities that come from the accidental powers of the soul are for us these. Anger is when a person is moved to take revenge on the one who has distressed and crushed him. Desire is when a person desires food, drink, intercourse,

possessions, and other such things. Perception through the five senses is the discernment of bodily and sensible things: of colors and shapes through sight; of sound and melodies through hearing; of fragrant and foul odors through smell; of sweet and bitter food and drink and the like through taste; of smooth and rough, hot and cold, and the like through touch. Imagination is that which, as it were in abundance [?], fashions false fancies, as when a person often imagines someone flying, or a fish walking on land.

1. The natural powers of the soul: Intellect: that which knows things not through words, nor through demonstrations, nor even through teachings, but through hidden and simple vision. Understanding: that which knows things through words, demonstrations, teachings and syllogisms. Cognition: [?] Rationality: that which distinguishes true thoughts from false ones. Self-motion: from itself, not from another. Memory: that which gathers knowledge and what has been learned.
2. The accidental powers of the soul: Anger: that a person is moved to take revenge on the one who distressed him. Desire: that a person desires food, drink, intercourse and possessions. Perception: that which, through the five senses, is the discernment of bodily and sensible things, through sight, hearing, smell and taste. Imagination: that which, as it were in abundance [?], fashions false fancies.

We must therefore investigate why these powers are so called: why intellect, I mean, and understanding, cognition, rationality, self-motion and memory are called natural powers of the soul, while anger

and desire, perception through the five senses, and imagination are called accidental powers of the soul. We say that those called natural are so called for these reasons: (1) first, because they come from the nature of the soul and not from anywhere else; (2) because they are naturally fixed in the nature of the soul; (3) because they constitute the nature of the soul; (4) because they are included in the definitions of the soul, and by them it is distinguished from other natures; (5) because when they are present to the soul they benefit its subsistence, and if it happens that they depart from it, or even one of them does, they impair it; (6) because they belong to it singly and properly, the body having no share in them. The other four, however — anger, desire, discernment through the five senses, and imagination — are called accidental powers of the soul because they do not belong to the soul, nor are they fixed and planted in its nature, but belong to the body and its temperaments; and because, being joined with the body, they befall the soul and it receives them on account of its being bound to it. That these powers do not belong to the soul is known from these proofs. First, they are not included in the definitions of the soul

when it is defined, for its definition contains neither anger nor desire, nor discernment through the senses, nor imagination. (2) Because the soul was created in the image of God, and these things are not in God. (3) Because holy men have overcome and conquered desire and anger. Therefore the five senses and the four powers do not belong to the soul but to the body and its temperaments. (4) And that this is so is known from the fact that anger and desire are found in irrational animals as well; likewise discernment through the five senses is found in them, though not rational discernment. For they have the bodily discernment of the five senses, but not a rational one such as human beings have.

We must further investigate how these powers befall the soul from the body, because it is bound to it and shares in it. We say thus: the soul is incorporeal, and there are sensible and visible natures in this world, which are bodies; and when it deals with them through the mediation of the body, which is a body, these powers befall it. For instance, we say that some bodies are harmful and some beneficial. And when, through the body, it comes into contact with those

harmful bodies, it is hurt by them, embittered and angered; and in this way the irascible power befalls it. And when, through the body, it draws near to those pleasant bodies, it is gratified and loves them and desires them; and in this way the desiring power befalls it. And because it deals with all bodies through the mediation of the body's five senses, there befalls it the power that is perception through the five senses. And because imagination is born of perception through the five senses, imagination too befalls the soul. From the things that sight, hearing, smell and touch discern, a person rises up and imagines and fashions false fancies, as it were in abundance [?]. For example, from seeing an eagle flying, he imagines a donkey that [?], and imagines a man flying. And from things that are near to the senses he imagines things that are far away. Therefore imagination is born of perception through the five senses.
Of the powers, some belong to the soul by nature: intellect, understanding, cognition, rationality, self-motion, memory. Others belong to the body (and because it is compounded with the soul, they befall the soul as well): anger, desire, perception, imagination.

Now someone may object and say that in many places certain philosophers have said that the powers of the soul are three: rationality, anger and desire. To such a person we say: in what they said about rationality being a power of the soul, they were right, for rationality is a power of the soul, as we showed above. But as for his saying that anger and desire are powers of the soul, one of two things befalls them. Either they missed the truth in this and spoke falsely; or they did not miss the truth but erred — either in the imposition of names, in that by homonymy they took "soul" simply and did not divide it into its different significations, and so went wrong; or they called these powers of the soul although they do not belong to the soul but to the body, because they befall the soul too and so are called accidental powers of the soul, as we showed in the theories above.

Showing that the soul is rational and self-moving — that is, moved by itself and not by another —

and ever-moving — that is, perpetually moved, never resting from its motion. That the soul is rational is known from the fact that it distinguishes true thoughts from false thoughts. For this is how philosophers define rationality: as a power that discerns thoughts. If rationality is a power that discerns thoughts, and the soul has a power that discerns thoughts, then the soul has rationality; and if it has rationality, it is clearly rational. It is also known that it is self-moving — that is, moved by itself — from these arguments. First: man is composed of two natures, and it is the soul that moves the body rationally. If, then, the soul moves the body, and there is no third thing that moves it, then it is moved by itself; for that which is moved and also moves another, when there is no other that moves it, is itself moved by itself. (2) It is known from this: that which lives of itself and not from another is moved by itself and not by another. The soul is life in its nature and lives of itself, not from another. Therefore it is moved by itself and not by another. (3) It is known

from this: if the body is not moved rationally by itself but by the soul, it is clear that the soul is moved by itself and not by another, because the powers of the soul are opposed to those of the body, as the great one among the apostles, Paul, said: "The spirit desires what harms the body," and likewise conversely. If, then, the body is not moved rationally by itself, while the soul is moved by itself, the soul is further known to be ever-moving — that is, perpetually moved, never resting from its motion — from these proofs. 1. From the fact that it is moved by itself; and that which is moved by itself does not rest from its motion. The soul is moved by itself. Therefore it does not rest from its motion but is perpetually moved. (2) From the fact that the body is at one time moved and at another rests from its motion, while the powers of the soul are opposed to those of the body. Therefore the soul is perpetually moved without resting from its motion. (3) From the fact that man has two words: one the inner word fixed within, and the other the uttered word. The fixed word is born from the soul, while the uttered word is completed in the body. And the word

that is born from the soul is not thinking, as some have supposed and said, but is the power that discerns thoughts. For this word that is born from the soul we call rationality, that is, this power. Or rather, this word is neither thinking nor a thought, for two reasons. First, because this word distinguishes true thoughts from false ones, and thoughts are discerned by it; and what discerns is different from what is discerned by it, just as the saw is different from the planks: the one cuts, while the others are cut. And it is known from the fact that thoughts cut one another off and are cut off from one another, whereas this word neither cuts itself off nor is cut off from itself. Therefore the word that is born from the soul is not thinking but rationality, that is, the power that discerns thoughts. The uttered word, on the other hand, is the one that is heard and completed in the body, that is, by the mouth, tongue, palate, teeth and lips, as air enters the throat and comes out again. Therefore human beings have two words: one

that is born from the soul, which is the fixed word; and the other that is completed in the body, which is the uttered word, at one time in motion and at another at rest. But the fixed word is perpetually in motion and never rests from its motion; for even if someone wished to hold it back from its motion for a single blink of the eye, he could not. Therefore, just as this fixed word is ever-moving, and just as the uttered word at one time [rests] and at another does not, so too the body in which it is completed is at one time moved and at another not. Therefore it has been shown by these arguments that the soul is ever-moving and moves perpetually.

Showing in how many ways motion is spoken of, which motion we say the soul has, what the motion of the soul is, and what the definition of this motion is. The philosopher Aristotle said in his book On the Categories that motion is spoken of in six ways: two in substance, two in quantity, one in quality, and another in place. In substance,

as in generation and corruption. In generation, as with human seed that is sown and from which the complete human body comes into being. In corruption, as with the human body that is moved and corrupted through death. In quantity, as in growth and diminution. In growth, as with grass that is moved and grows in size. In diminution, as with grass that is sown and diminishes in size. In quality, the motion that occurs in the alteration of a body or living body that is moved and changes from whiteness to blackness and from blackness to whiteness. Motion in place is this: movement from position to position. This is divided sevenfold: up and down, to the right and to the left, forward and backward — as when someone shoots an arrow or throws a stone toward one of these six ends … — and also circular, as with the millstone that is moved and turns in a circle.

Motion is spoken of in six ways: As in generation: as a seed that becomes a body. As in corruption: as a body that is corrupted. As in growth: as grass that grows. As in diminution: as a tree that diminishes. As in alteration: as a body that becomes black or white. As in change from position to position: upward, as fire that blazes upward; downward, as waters that flow downward; to the right, as an arrow that is shot; to the left, forward, backward, as toward one of these ends; circularly, as a millstone that is moved.

In which of these modes of motion is the soul moved? We say: not in that of change from position to position, nor in that of growth and diminution, nor in that of corruption, because these modes of motion apply only to bodies, which are moved in them. For bodies

grow and diminish in size, bodies change from position to position, and bodies are corrupted. But the soul is incorporeal; therefore it is not moved in these modes of motion. Nor is it moved in the mode of motion that is generation, because it came into being all at once, and is not like human seed, which is moved little by little and becomes the complete human body. Therefore the soul is not moved in these five modes of motion, not even in one of them. It remains, then, that the soul is moved in the mode of motion that is "as in [?] alteration." That this is so is known from the fact that this motion, called "as in alteration," is spoken of both bodies and incorporeal things. So, just as the body is moved and changes from whiteness to blackness and from blackness to whiteness, so too the soul is moved and changes from evil to good and from good to evil, from fear and from joy, from ignorance to knowledge, from learning to forgetfulness, and from forgetfulness

to remembrance. We must therefore investigate what the motion of the soul is. We say that the motion of the soul is a power — a spiritual power by which it is moved perpetually and without rest toward knowledge and teachings, toward thoughts and their discernment, toward virtue and vice, courage, fear and joy, and toward the rest of such things. It remains, further, to say what the definition of motion is. We say that the definition of motion is the path from power to activity. Take an example of this. Intellect is a power of the soul, and the activity of this power is to know things not through demonstrations and words but through simple and hidden knowledge. Motion, then, is the path and passage from this power to this activity. Understand it in the same way for the rest of the powers and activities of the soul. This becomes still clearer from the diagram drawn below:
Soul: Intellect: knowing things without words. Understanding: knowing things through words. Rationality: discerning thoughts.

Showing that the soul is capable of thought. The soul is capable of thought, and this is known from these arguments. 1. From the knowledge and crafts that human beings have discovered, in that they discovered them through the thoughts of the soul, and not by chance or haphazardly. 2. From the fact that we first form things in our thoughts before we acquire them, something the senses of our body do not show us. For the carpenter first forms in his thought the chair and its shape before he makes it; and likewise the architect first forms the house in his mind before he builds it. 3. It is known that the soul is capable of thought from the fact that we cannot see the nature of events with the senses, and so we contemplate it and know it by the thoughts of the soul. Therefore the soul is capable of thought.

Showing how many and which properties the soul has. One property of the soul, then, is this: that of all beings, created and rational, it alone

needs to make use of deliberative thought and, by turning its thoughts over, to weigh whether it ought to do something or not. (2) It is the one that, while bound in the body, its companion and dwelling, meditates on things far away and sees them in imagination as if they were near, without leaving or going away from its dwelling. (3) It is also the one that, when the body to which it is bound sleeps, rests along with it; and because of the bond by which it is held, it is prevented from doing the things it was occupied with while awake. (4) It is the one that, while bound in the body, suffers with it in its sufferings and is distressed by its pains, although by nature it is not subject to suffering. (5) That is, it is the one that hates iniquity and loves righteousness, even if it slips, stumbles and sins. These are its properties. (6) It is the one that discovers various arts and inventive knowledge. Here there is an outline of the powers and properties of the soul, but in the preceding section we recalled more [?]

Showing what the definition of the soul is, and what it is like. We say, then, that the definition of the soul is this: a living substance, immortal, intelligent, reasoning, knowing, remembering, self-moving, luminous, subtle, pure, light, invisible, united to the body, separated from it in time, and [?] united to it inseparably. Because we called it a living substance [?]. By the other terms we have indicated its natural powers and its essential differences, which are explained to us in the theories above. But here we speak of them together with the rest of the terms.

So when we called it luminous, we do not mean that it has the light of the sun or the flame of a lamp, but that it is illumined in the knowledge of things and matters. When we called it subtle, we do not mean in the manner of subtle bodies that can be perceived, which by [?] toward the portion opposite to dense bodies, but that it escapes the things by which the body is perceived. Pure, because its nature never receives the uncleanness of the body, which is bodily. Light, because it never has a tendency to sink downward. Invisible, because it is incorporeal and does not have three dimensions. And by saying that it is united to a body, that is, to the body, it is distinguished from the angels, who are not united to bodies. The definition of the soul is made known more clearly from this division: Substance: substance is the genus of the definition. Living: the nature of the soul. Immortal: the nature of the soul. Intelligent: a power of the soul. Remembering: a power of the soul. Knowing: a power of the soul. Self-moving: a power of the soul.

Luminous: a difference of the soul from bodies. Subtle: a difference of the soul from bodies. Pure: a difference of the soul from bodies. Light: a difference of the soul from bodies. Invisible: a difference of the soul from bodies. United to the body: a difference of the soul from bodies. Showing that the soul is immortal. That the soul is immortal is truly known from these demonstrations. 1: Everything that exists is either simple or composite. Where there is composition, there is also contrariety; there is also strife and conflict. Where there is conflict, there is dissolution and separation. And where there is dissolution and separation, there is also death. But where there is simplicity, there is no composition; and where there is no composition, neither is there contrariety; and where there is no contrariety, there is no conflict or strife.

And where there is no conflict, there is no dissolution or separation; and where there is no dissolution, neither is there death. Therefore, where there is simplicity, there is no death. It is known, then, that the soul is immortal from the fact that it is simple, as follows: the soul is simple, and what is simple does not die, because where there is simplicity there is no death. 2: From the fact that it is living and perpetually in motion. The soul, then, is perpetually in motion, and what lives by motion does not come to an end; it does not die. Therefore the soul does not die. 3: From the fact that the soul does not sleep; for even while the body [?], it does what it does. For the soul does not sleep, and what does not sleep does not die. Therefore the soul does not die. Indeed, one of the teachers said that the soul does not die because the soul does not sleep. 4: From the fact that it is life by its nature. The soul, then, is life by its nature; what has life as its nature does not die. Therefore the soul is immortal. 5: It is known that the soul does not die from the fact that the body dies. For it is the body's opposite, and if the body dies, the soul necessarily does not die, since it is its opposite. The body dies, and the soul is the opposite of the body. Therefore

the soul does not die. 6: It is known that it does not die from the fact that the body is sustained by its goods and destroyed by its evils. The goods of the body are beauty, health, a good temperament and soundness of limbs. These excellences sustain the body; so the body's goods sustain it. But the soul is not sustained by its goods, nor is it destroyed by its evils. Its goods are righteousness, virtue, purity, joy and the like. Its evils are iniquity, envy, lewdness, hatred, grief and the like. If the soul is not sustained by its goods and is not destroyed by its evils, then it does not die. 7: There are three kinds of corruption. One is the dissolution of compounds, as in the dissolution of the structure of a house or a ship: dissolution destroys the house and the ship. Another is division and cutting into parts, as with a beam of ten cubits that is divided and cut into parts and small pieces: so division and cutting destroy it when it is cut. Another is that which comes about through the change of a thing,

when it is destroyed from what it is and becomes something else, as with human seed, which is destroyed from being seed and becomes a body. So corruption comes about in three ways: 1: the dissolution of a compound, like the dissolution of a house; 2: the cutting of a thing, like the division of a beam; 3: the change of a thing, like seed that is destroyed and becomes a body. Since none of these three kinds of corruption affects the soul, the soul does not die. 8: From the fact that it moves the body. For if the body, which is moved, is mortal, the soul, which moves it, does not die. It is known that it does not die from this: two kinds of suffering befall a human being, one, I mean, upon the body, and another upon the soul. That of the body is a wound, a cut, lashes, or a sore, pain and the like. That of the soul is sin, guilt, folly, deficiencies,

error [?] or the like. The sufferings of the body, which are wounds, cuts and the rest, are not kept for retribution, because the body in which they subsist is dissolved. But the sufferings of the soul, which are sin, guilt and the rest, are kept for retribution, because the soul in which they subsist is not dissolved and does not die. 9: It is known that the soul does not die from this line of reasoning: there is negligence; and if there is negligence, there is necessarily also judgment; and if there is judgment, there is also one who is judged; and if there is one who is judged, there is necessarily also an immortal soul. These demonstrations come from natural and rational proofs, which show that the soul is immortal. And the testimonies from the holy scriptures which confirm that the soul does not die are these. God said to Moses: "I am the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob." And God is not the God of the dead but of the living. By saying that God is not the God of the dead but of the living, he showed that their souls are not dead but living. And Solomon said: "The body returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit to the Lord

who gave it." By saying that the spirit [does not] return to the earth as the body returns, he showed that it is incorruptible; and by saying that it returns and goes back to the Lord, he made known that it does not die but lives. Again, our Lord said in the Gospel: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." By saying that they cannot kill it, he showed two things: first, that the soul is incorporeal; second, that it is immortal. Incorporeal, because it cannot receive the sufferings that befall the body, which is a bodily thing; immortal, because it is not destroyed (killed) like the body. Again, he said in the story of the rich man and Lazarus that after the rich man died and was buried, the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham's bosom, and that the rich man asked Abraham for water, and so on. By saying that the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham's bosom, and by Abraham's answering the rich man as he did, he showed through all this that souls are living and never

die. Again, the divine apostle Paul speaks of the body thus: "This corruptible is to put on incorruption, [and this] mortal [immortality]." It is as if he were holding the body in his hand and pointing to it with his finger when he said, "this corruptible and mortal." And by saying of the body "this corruptible and mortal," he showed that the soul is incorruptible and does not die. Therefore the soul is immortal. Showing in what sense we apply these names to the soul, "immortal" and "incorporeal," when we say them of it: as privation or as possession. There are names which, when they are spoken, seem to signify privation, though they signify not privation but possession. And again there are names which, when they are spoken, seem to signify possession, though they signify not possession but privation. As follows: those which seem to signify privation, though they signify not privation but possession, are these: incorporeal, irrational, immortal, soulless,

and the like. And those which seem to signify possession, though they signify not possession but privation, are these: sickness, nakedness, poverty, blindness, evil, darkness and the like. Sickness is the privation of health; nakedness is the privation of clothing; poverty is the privation of wealth; blindness is the privation of sight; darkness is the privation of light; and evil is the privation of good. But those privative names, I mean incorporeal, immortal, irrational, soulless and the rest, signify two things alike: both what is inferior to that of which they are the privation, and what surpasses it. As follows: when they say "incorporeal," they do not strip it of anything; rather we indicate one of two things: either something inferior to a body, such as matter alone, or form alone, or such as qualities and kinds, for these

are all incorporeal, being inferior to bodies; or else we signify something superior to bodies when we say "incorporeal," such as angels and souls, which are incorporeal because they surpass bodies. Therefore "incorporeal" signifies not privation but possession, which is either inferior to that of which it was the privation, or superior to it.
