So too with "immortal": when we say "immortal," we signify not privation but two kinds of possession: one, of stones and beams, which are inferior to man, who is mortal; the other, of angels and the soul, which are superior to man, who is mortal, and from whom the privation was taken. In this same way, then, when we say "irrational" and "soulless." It has thus been shown that when we call the soul immortal and incorporeal, we do not strip it of anything by these names; rather we indicate possession. For by calling it immortal we signify that it is life, since its nature is life, as we showed above; and by calling it incorporeal we indicate that it surpasses the body. Therefore these names, "immortal" and "incorporeal,"

when we say them of the soul, signify possession and not privation. Showing that the soul is not cut and is not divided into parts. The soul is not cut, nor is it divided into parts. And this is known from the following. 1: The soul is incorporeal, and what is incorporeal is not cut, nor is it divided into parts; it is body that is cut and divided into parts. Therefore the soul is not cut, nor is it divided into parts. 2: For just as the soul does not become paralyzed along with bodies whose hands and feet are paralyzed, nor blind along with blind bodies, nor deaf and [?] along with deaf and [?] bodies, so it is not cut along with hands and feet that are cut off, or with other limbs of the body that are cut off. Therefore the soul is not cut, nor is it divided into parts. But if someone objects and says, "If the soul is not cut along with the limbs when they are cut, why does a limb run, twitch and move after it has been cut off?", we say that the limb that was cut off feels this, not because the rational soul was cut off with it, but because there was cut off with it the sensory and motive power that irrational animals and bodies also have.

Showing that the soul governs the body. Someone asks, saying: Which of them governs the other, and which is governed by the other? Does the soul govern the body, or the body the soul? We say that it is the soul that governs the body, and this is known from these demonstrations. 1: From the fact that the body is its instrument, and through it the soul does good and evil, and through it is justified and sins; and whoever works with an instrument governs the instrument. Therefore the soul governs the body. 2: It is known that the soul governs it from the fact that it often restrains it from its desire. For sometimes the body desires to eat, to drink, to sleep and to have intercourse, and the soul reins it in from its desire. And sometimes people's bodies are seized by burning fevers and they long for a cold drink, and because it would harm them, the rational soul keeps them from drinking. Therefore it governs the body. 3: Often, when a craftsman has set himself a goal, he misses it and then goes back to correct it, as follows: sometimes, when an architect has set himself the goal of raising a house ten cubits, he raises it twelve. This happened because the thought of the soul did not keep pace with the movement of the body, nor did the reason of the soul restrain

the body's movement toward building twelve cubits. So he missed his goal, though not intentionally [?]. And then he goes back to correct the thing in which he went wrong, by means of the same body and by means of the same hands. Because of these things it is known that the soul governs the body. 4: During the movement of contemplation the body is at rest, and when contemplation is finished, the body then brings forth through action what accords with the movement of contemplation. And since contemplation belongs to the soul, the soul's action comes about through contemplation. Therefore the soul indeed governs the body. 5: The great one among the apostles, Paul, said: "I subdue my body and make it my slave." In this one saying he showed three things: first, that Paul himself is the soul; second, that his body is the instrument of his soul, since he calls it "my body"; and third, that his soul governed the body. For he did not say, "My body subdues me" or "governs me," but "I, who am the soul, subdue my body and make it my slave." And if the soul subdues and enslaves, while the body is subdued and enslaved, then the soul governs the body, as the true and divine apostle

Paul said. Truly, then, it is the soul that enables the body to move, to act rationally and to live rationally. Showing in how many senses anything that differs from another is said to differ; whether souls differ from one another or not; and by what difference souls differ from one another. Anything that differs from another either differs from it by itself or differs from it by some other difference. What differs from another by itself is, for example, whiteness and blackness: whiteness differs by itself from blackness, that is, by what it is, it differs from white. What differs from another by a difference other than the things that differ is spoken of in many senses. This difference is either essential, or accidental, or hypostatic. Essential, such as rationality and irrationality: for a man differs from a donkey by rationality, and likewise a donkey differs from a man by irrationality. The accidental difference is spoken of in two ways: it is either separable or inseparable. Separable,

such as standing and sitting, motion and rest: for Socrates differs from Plato because the one is standing and the other sitting; Socrates is moving and Plato is at rest. Inseparable, such as being grey-eyed and being snub-nosed: Anytus, who is grey-eyed, differs from Meletus, who is not grey-eyed; and Meletus, who is snub-nosed, differs from Anytus, who is not snub-nosed. The hypostatic difference is that of the characteristic properties of a hypostasis. These properties are living, characteristic and individual, such as unbegottenness, which is the property of Adam, and procession, which is the property of Eve. For Adam differs from Eve by [un]begottenness, and Eve differs from Adam and from Seth by procession. For God created and established Adam without begetting; Eve he created and established by procession from Adam's rib, which he took out of his side; and Seth God created and established by begetting from Adam and Eve. These kinds of differences are made known from the division written below. For example, smoothness differs from roughness by itself, and thought differs by itself, that is, by what it is.

Everything that differs from another: either it differs from it by itself; essential: such as mortality and immortality: for a man differs from an angel by mortality, and likewise an angel differs from a man by immortality. Or accidental: either separable: such as silence and speech: for Socrates, who is speaking, differs from Plato, who is silent, and Plato, who is silent, differs from Socrates, who is speaking. Or inseparable: such as baldness, or a scar left by a boil: Anytus, who is bald, differs from Meletus, who is not bald, and Meletus, who has a scar, differs from Anytus, who has no scar. Or hypostatic: such as characteristic and individual properties: Adam differs from Seth by unbegottenness, Seth differs from Adam and Eve by begottenness, and likewise Eve differs from both of them by procession.

Let us now inquire about souls, whether they differ from one another or do not differ from one another. 1: Souls are many, and many things differ from one another. If souls did not differ from one another, they would be found to be one and not many; but that they are one is false, and that they are many is true. Therefore, if they are many, they are all different. 2: If they did not differ from one another, the soul of Peter would not be distinct from that of Paul, nor that of Socrates from that of Plato. And if they did not differ and were not distinct from one another, there would be great confusion. Therefore souls differ from one another. By what difference do they differ from one another? We say that they do not differ from one another by the essential difference, because they are all rational and immortal, and their essential powers are also equal to one another and they do not differ in them; for all of them are intelligent, knowing, discerning, remembering and self-moving. So too in the rest of their natural powers they are equal to one another and do not differ. Therefore souls do not differ from one another by the essential difference, nor by some other difference apart from themselves.

Likewise, souls too differ from one another by themselves, and not by other differences that are apart from them. Therefore souls differ from one another by themselves, that is, by what they are, just as angels differ from one another by themselves. And again we say that they also differ from one another in number, in that one is the first, this one the second, another the third, another the fourth, and so on. Showing whether souls, when they depart from the body, acquire another difference besides the one we have spoken of, namely that they differ from one another by themselves and also in number, or not. We have shown that souls differ by themselves and also in number, as angels differ from one another, and as thoughts, understanding, reflections and visions differ from one another. Someone may ask and say: When souls depart from bodies, do they acquire another difference besides this one, or not? And we say that, since each one of them, when they depart from their bodies, comes to be in spiritual places suited to their nature, they therefore again differ from one another by another difference,

I mean in incorporeal accidents, which are the righteousness and iniquity they practiced here. For just as incorporeal accidents, such as whiteness, blackness, snub-nosedness, grey-eyedness and the like, subsist in bodies, which are corporeal, so too righteousness and iniquity, which are incorporeal accidents, subsist in souls, which are incorporeal. Therefore souls, when they depart from bodies, come to differ from one another in two further differences: I mean in spiritual place, and also in incorporeal accidents, which are righteousness and iniquity. Therefore we say that while souls are in bodies, they differ by themselves and also in number; and when they depart from bodies, they come to differ also in places, in righteousness and in iniquity. So when they depart from bodies they differ from one another in four differences: by themselves, in number, in place, and in righteousness and iniquity. For example, the soul of Peter the apostle and that of Simon the sorcerer differ by themselves, in that the individuality of the one is other than

the individuality of the other. They also differ in number, since the one is one and the other is the second. The two also differ in place, for Peter's soul dwells with the angels, but Simon's with the demons until the day of resurrection. And they also differ in incorporeal accidents, because the one is righteous and holy, and the other unrighteous and wicked. Inquiring about souls united to flesh, those of infants who were miscarried before they were formed in a likeness and completed in their limbs. Someone asks about souls united to flesh, those which were miscarried and came out of the womb before they were formed in a likeness or completed in their limbs, and whose souls were released from them and separated: are these souls like the souls that were with bodies until childhood and youth, or until old age, or do they differ and are they distinct from them? And we say that they are like them in everything: whether in nature, or in being incorporeal and immortal, or in the rest of the natural powers, or in the differences they acquire, they are alike, except for this alone, that they differ

from them in that they have acquired no deeds, whether good or evil, and do not remember having done anything here. Consider the souls of infants who are separated from their bodies in infancy in the same way. Concerning the soul: where it comes from. Someone here raises a question, saying: Where does the soul come from? And we say to him that Mani, Marcion, Bardaisan and others with them say that the soul is from the nature of God, that is, a part of his being. Others say that the soul is born, brought forth and flows from a soul. Others say that the soul is born and brought forth from the seed of the man. Where the soul comes from: Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan say that it is from the nature of God; others say that the soul is born, brought forth and flows from a soul; others say that it is brought forth and born from the seed of the man. And first we reply to those who say that

the soul is from the nature of God. But it is not true that the soul is from the nature of God, and this is known from these demonstrations. 1: The nature of God is unchangeable, but the soul changes in righteousness and iniquity, in joy and sorrow. Therefore the soul is not from the nature of God. 2: The soul exists by the will of God; but of God's nature it is not said that it exists by the will of God, nor that it exists not by the will of God; rather, because it is his nature, it is said to exist. Therefore the soul is not from the nature of God. 3: The soul receives teaching and learns; the nature of God does not receive teachings, because it is perfect in all things and lacks nothing. 4: The soul has no foreknowledge. Therefore the soul is not from the nature of God. 5: Moses said that God formed Adam and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Now one who blows does not blow from his own nature; it is air that he draws in and contains within himself and brings into the lungs, and so he blows it out with his breath. How much more, then, did God the Maker not breathe from his own nature when he breathed into Adam! Nor did he draw in air and blow as we do, for he is not corporeal and is above organic instruments

and blowing. Therefore the soul is not from the nature of God. 6: It is known again that the soul is not from the nature of God from the absurdity to which this leads, thus: if the soul is from the nature of God, and the soul is cut off from him and dwells in the body, then the nature of God is divisible. 7: If the soul is from the nature of God, and souls are many, then the nature of God has many parts. 8: If the soul is from the nature of God, and the soul is different, then the nature of God differs from it; and if so, it is composite; and if it is composite, it is created. 9: If the soul is from the nature of God, and the soul sins in thought and is judged, then God himself sins and he himself judges, and he is found to sin against himself, to judge himself, and to be condemned and punished. These are absurdities to think of God. It has therefore been shown by these arguments that the soul is not from the nature of God. These, then, are against those who say that the soul is from the nature of God. Against those who say that the soul is from a soul, and is born, flows and is brought forth from it. That this is not true is known from the following. 1: If, then, a body flows, is born and is brought forth from a body,

the soul, which is incorporeal... We say that the soul is never born from a soul, nor is it brought forth or flows from one. And this is known from the following. If, then, a body flows, is born and is brought forth from a body, the soul, which is incorporeal, cannot flow, be born or be brought forth from another incorporeal soul, because the soul is the opposite of the body, just as the body is the opposite of the incorporeal. So since body is born from body, soul is never born from soul. 2: It is known, then, that the incorporeal is not brought forth from the incorporeal from the angels and demons, who do not bear offspring; so too soul is not born from soul. 3: The soul is simple and is not divided into parts, and what is simple and not divided into parts neither begets nor is begotten. Therefore soul is not born from soul, nor is it brought forth. But if someone objects and says, "Look, God the Father is simple and does not admit division into parts, yet he begot the Son and brought forth the Spirit," we say to him that God the Father begot the Son and brought forth the Spirit eternally and by nature, and not by flowing and bringing forth one after another, which cannot apply to an incorporeal nature but only to bodies. 4: If the soul is born and brought forth, then it is mortal,

and corruption attaches to it, as it attaches to bodies that are born from bodies and beget from them. Therefore soul is not born from soul. These, again, are against those who say that soul is born and brought forth from soul. Against those who say that the soul is born and brought forth from the seed of the man, we say that it is not true, and this is known from the following. 1: If the soul is incorporeal, it cannot be born from the seed of the man, which is a body. If the incorporeal is not born from the incorporeal, neither is it born from a body. 2: If the seed of the man is the cause and begetter of the soul, and the soul is incorporeal, then the seed of the man is incorporeal, which is false. Therefore the soul is not from the seed of the man, nor is it born or brought forth from it. It has thus been clearly shown by all these arguments that the soul is not from the nature of God, nor is it born and brought forth from another soul, nor is it born from the seed of the man. Where, then, does the soul come from? We say that God created it from nothing; and that he did not create it from something is known from the following. 1: Body and the incorporeal are opposites of one another. And if God created the body, which is bodily, from something, because

its opposite, which is incorporeal, God created from nothing, since it is incorporeal. 2. Just as He created the angels from nothing, so too He created, and still creates, souls from nothing. 3. For just as He created Adam's body from something (and by this I also mean bodies that come from human seed), and just as He created Adam's soul from nothing, so too He creates from nothing all the souls that come after Adam's soul, until the end of the world. For Adam's soul is equal in nature to the souls that came after it. 4. That God creates souls from nothing is known from the words of Zechariah, who says of God: "He forms the spirit of man within him." Since it is formed, as the prophet says, we know that He created it from nothing, for whatever is formed is formed from nothing. Our Lord also says in the Gospel: "(My Father) is working until now, and I too am working." So by saying "and I too am working" He made three things known. The first is that He creates all things every hour and every day, and in creating ......... equal in nature to those that were created. Since He continually creates souls every day from nothing, this is one sense of His saying

"and I too am working." The second is that He takes care of His creation in winter and summer, at sowing and harvest, in striking and killing, and so on. The third sense is that He preserves His creatures. An inquiry into how the soul is created: within the body or outside the body. In the previous chapter we showed that the soul is created from nothing. Let us now investigate where the Lord creates the soul: within the body or outside it. We say that some people hold that He creates it within the body. This is known from three things. The first is

that if He created it outside the body and then brought it in and united it with the body, it ought to remember its nature as it was without a body, and the things it was among before it entered the body. Yet we see that it remembers nothing of the kind. The second is that if He created it outside the body and brought it in, it would not have ...... love and harmony with the body, because it would see its own loftiness and superiority and the lowliness and inferiority of the body. So one of two things would have happened. Either it would not have entered the body at all, or it would not merely lack love for the body but would actually feel hatred toward it. Yet we see that it has love and harmony with it. The third is known from the words of Zechariah the prophet, who says of God: "who forms the spirit of man within him." The prophet said that He forms it there. So what we say is true, they argue: God creates the soul within the human being. That is how some have thought and spoken about where the soul is created. The Greek teachers, however, say that God creates the soul outside the body, brings it into the body and unites it with it. Testimonies of the teachers on this chapter and the one before it, showing that the soul is created from nothing and that God creates it outside the body and brings it into the body. The holy Severus, in his letter to Peter the monk, who claimed that the soul is corruptible and gets its existence from seed, says this. Severus: "You said, in your eagerness to show that the soul is corruptible and gets its existence from seed, being sown together with the body, and there you cited the proof of Julian. He said that from the will (he reads 'of the man'), from the will of the man, a human being is breathed into the womb and lives, while the material emission of the seed gives power to the composite that receives it. Know that he does not say the soul gets its existence from the matter of the seed. He says that it comes together with the emission of the seed, and that the soul is created at the same moment. Gregory of Nyssa says the same in the third chapter of On the Making of Man: they do not precede one another, but [the soul] has [its beginning] at the very moment the seed is emitted [?]. And Cyril, in what he wrote against Diodore, says that in our understanding of man the soul and the body run equal courses with each other, but the soul is what brings [the body] to completion

and it is cast in from outside, and little by little it brings the one being conceived to its own activity. Gregory the Theologian shows this in his discourse in verse: 'The one part comes from body, from body; but the soul is mingled invisibly, entering from outside into the clay that is from the earth (the seed).' These passages are enough to show that the parents are the cause of the body only, not of the soul, and that the soul is immortal. It enters from outside together with the body, or at the emission of the seed, as God knows, who made our soul from the divine breath and mingled it with the body, and it is immortal and indissoluble. Dissolution belongs properly to the souls of animals. So it is clear that the parents are the cause of the body only, while the existence of the soul came from the divine breath." That same Peter the monk claimed that Cyril contradicts the Theologian, because Cyril says that the breath of which Moses spoke, when God breathed into Adam, is the Holy Spirit, while the Theologian says that this breath is the soul. The holy Severus answered him in that same letter,

a little before the passage we have quoted: "You say that Cyril says God made the body from the earth and gave it life with a rational and intelligent soul, in the way that He knows. And because it was fitting for man to share in the Holy Spirit, He breathed into him the spirit of life. This is the Spirit that is given to creatures and shapes their likeness after the divine likeness. And again in his third and fourth discourse he says: 'We do not say that the divine breath is the soul. If it were, the soul would be unchangeable, as having come forth from God. It is rather participation in the Holy Spirit, which was placed in the soul from the beginning; and because of this divine [gift] the rational living being came to be in the image of God. That is why Christ, when He renewed [man], breathed on His disciples.' Gregory the Theologian, on the other hand, says that the soul came from not being into being through the breath, because spiritual goodness was cast into the living being at that same moment. By it, they say, we live and move, since it is the abundant power of the breath, and the breaths

that are breathed in, and the Holy Spirit for those who [?]. In the same discourse, On the Nativity, he says again: 'He took the matter of the body, but from Himself He placed life in it, which the Word knows to be an intelligent soul and the image of God.' So the human soul was brought into being from the breath of God. It has been argued that Cyril says that, on the contrary, He breathed the Holy Spirit into the soul, while Gregory says that this breath was the soul." That is what Peter the monk said, and the holy Severus said this to him: "Consider that the people who questioned Cyril supposed that this breath was changed into a human being, not that the soul was created by the breath as if by a hand. Against their ignorance he said that the soul was not the breath, so that they would not imagine change or suffering in the whole divine essence. The soul came from the breath, in that the Spirit made the soul just as He made the heavenly powers. So Gregory speaks in the fuller sense when he says that the power of the breath is what gave the breath of life, and the Holy Spirit. Cyril, though, says that the image was being formed

when he is contending against their foolishness. So they do not contradict each other." We have quoted these words from the holy Severus. The holy Cyril says this: "The mother gave birth only to the flesh. God created the rational soul, as the prophet said: 'who forms the spirit of man within him.' But because of the natural and hypostatic union that the soul has with the body, she is called the mother who bore the whole human being." The holy Philoxenus, a Syrian teacher, also says in the fifth discourse: "With every woman, the flesh of the one born comes from her flesh and not from her soul, just as with the one born of the Virgin it was His body, and not His divinity." Theodoret of Cyrus also says in his book against the pagans: "From bodies He forms the bodies of living creatures, and from nothing, among the souls of all living creatures, only that of man." These are the testimonies of the teachers, and they show three things. The first is that the soul is created from nothing by the Creator's command. The second is that it is created outside the body and then enters bodies. The third is that parents beget the body only. Showing

whether the soul is created before the body, with the body, or after the body. Here too the questioner asks, investigating the soul, when it is created: before the body, with the body, or after the body. We say that the ancient pagans, Origen the heretic and others with them say that souls were created beforehand, before bodies, and because they turned away from the service of God they were cast into flesh as into a prison. The Syrian teachers, however, by whom I mean Mar Ephrem, Mar Jacob of Batnan, Philoxenus of Mabbug and Theodoret of Cyrus, along with the followers of Nestorius, all say that bodies are formed first and souls are created in them afterward from nothing. The Greek teachers reject both of these opinions. They say that the soul does not precede the body, nor the body the soul. Rather, the two come together at once and equally, in an instant that cannot be divided in time. The body takes shape from the man's seed, while the soul is created suddenly from nothing at the Creator's command. When is the soul created? Before the body, say the pagans. After the body, say the Syrian teachers. With the body, at once and equally, say the Greek teachers.

Let us then quote the words of Philoxenus, a Syrian teacher, who says in his book of commentary on the Gospel: "First the body is created and formed in all its members, and then the soul is created in it from nothing: in a male after forty days, and in a female after eighty days. So too Scripture, to let us know this, says elsewhere: 'A woman who has borne a male shall remain forty days in the blood of her purification,' as it commanded. It is as though during all those days she was carrying a dead body without a soul. And again elsewhere: 'If two men strike a pregnant woman and her child comes out, if harm has occurred, he shall surely pay; but if harm has not occurred, he shall be fined as much as the woman's husband imposes on him.' By 'if harm has occurred' it means the movement that comes to the body when the soul is created. By 'if harm has not occurred' it means that the infant had not yet moved at all through a soul. 'For the one who killed has killed, and has destroyed a human being; he shall surely be put to death.' But if movement had not yet come through the soul, the one who killed did not kill a living, rational human being, only a dead body, a soulless thing as it were. And if the soul had been prior [?] to the body,

Moses would not have said that God formed dust and only then breathed into his nostrils. Nor would Zechariah have said, 'who forms the spirit of man within him.'" These are the words of Philoxenus, who shows that the body is formed first and the soul is created in it afterward at the Creator's command. Mar Ephrem and Mar Jacob of Serug say the same in many places, and so do Theodoret of Cyrus and Nestorius the heretic. The Greek teachers, however, say that the soul does not precede the body, nor the body the soul. Rather, they come together into union at once and equally, the body being formed from something. Gregory the Theologian says in his discourse on the words of the Gospel: "I am afraid that some unfitting thought may creep in, as if the soul came down from some other place and was then bound in the body, and that because of how they lived there some received prophecy while others were condemned for having lived badly. But since this would be extremely loathsome and alien to the Church, let others toy with such teachings. For us it is not safe to dabble in things like these." And Gregory of Nyssa says in his discourse On the Making of Man: "Some of those before us, whose business was the discussion of first principles, thought it right to establish souls as a kind of nation

in a commonwealth of their own. There, too, it set before them examples of evil and of virtue. As long as the soul remains in the good, it stays untested by being joined with the body. But if it slips away from fellowship with the good toward the life here below, it slips into the body as well. Hence those who say that it existed before the body claim that it came to the body as if to a prison. Others, relying on Moses' account of the making of man, say that the soul is second to the body in time: first [man] was formed as a body, and afterward the soul came through the breath. So the soul, they say, came to be for the sake of the body, to give it movement. But whatever comes to be for the sake of something [is inferior to it], whereas the Gospel says that the soul is more than food and the body more than clothing. For this reason the argument of both these opinions is open to blame. We say that the soul does not come before the body, nor the body before the soul. Think of a grain of wheat: we say that the whole ear is contained in it, dwelling there in potency, the stalk, the fruit and the [?]. We do not say that any of these comes before another in the hidden account of its nature and was added to the nature of the seed afterward. Rather, nature reveals, in a certain order, the power placed in the seed, and no other nature is added to it from outside. In the same way

human seed too is sown from the first cause, and the power of nature unfolds and displays its existence as it extends through the natural sequence that brings it to completion, so that, as the saying goes, what is its own is its own and what comes from it comes from it. Those who opposed that first argument teach that [the soul] is older than the powers in the body and the conduct of the soul [?]. I do not think they are free of the teaching of the pagans, and for that reason they are likened to them. For if anyone examines these views carefully, he will find that their argument slides all the way into what the pagans say: that one of their wise men claimed that, though he was a man, he put on the body of a woman, flew with the birds, sprouted with the trees, and lived the life of creatures in the waters." The holy Cyril, in his book of commentary on the Gospel of John, where he examines the saying "which enlightens every man who comes into the world," overturned forceful arguments and strongly defended this confession: that souls do not come first, nor do bodies come before souls. And Andronicus, bishop of Gogra, in the book entitled The Poverty of Knowledge Falsely So Called, says this: "Sufficiently, then,

did the Lord teach not only that souls endure without passing away, but also that the form of the body is that by which they are distinguished as they are preserved, and that they remember the deeds of this world. He did this in the story He told about the rich man and Lazarus, who was resting in Abraham's bosom." The holy Severus says in his letter to Simus [?]: "When man was made, the rational soul was not created first, before the body, nor was the body formed before the soul. But some say that because Scripture says God formed Adam and afterward breathed into him, the forming came first and the giving of the soul comes second in order. Know, however, that Scripture tells of these divine things in human words. It cannot narrate everything at once, and in the poverty of words it cannot show or grasp the meaning of things that are beyond all matter and speech. Know that that first command and the swiftness of the will is the completion of what is created. And we find the same Scripture speaking of everything together when it says to Job: 'Did you take clay of the earth, and form a rational living being, and set it on the earth?' By these words it showed that the giving of the soul ran together with the forming. Therefore the divine breath was the making of the human soul."

Again, the holy Jacob of Edessa says in his letter to John the Stylite: "To this day my opinion is firmly settled that the soul does not precede the body in its creation, nor does the body precede the soul. For if anyone were to think anything of that kind, it would be utterly rejected [?] and outside our fold. Both of these are rejected heresies: the one that says souls come before bodies, as the pagans say, and the one that says bodies come before souls and souls are created for their sake. Rather, by a quick command bodies and souls were, and are, created together. However, you should know that the soul has three powers, or rather three kinds of soul, so to speak. One is the nourishing and growing soul, which is also called the vegetative. Another is the sensing and moving soul, which is also called elemental [?] or animal. The third is the rational and thinking soul, which we call the human soul, fashioned after the image of God. So we say that all three of these powers or kinds are in the human soul, or rather that the human soul is all of them: the nourishing and growing power, the sensing and moving power, and rational, thinking life. There are some teachers,

Greek or Syrian, who looked at the changes of these three powers or kinds of soul and said that the activities of these powers are revealed by degrees, little by little, in a certain order. The vegetative and growing power appears at the emission of the seed. A little after it comes the sensing and moving power. And after this, all at once, the rational and thinking power, partly before birth and gradually after birth. This gradation, this before and after, and this manifestation of these powers they called the soul [?]. Scripture too speaks of this concerning those who, in a quarrel, strike women and cause them to miscarry: if the child is formed, he shall pay a life as the price of a life; but if not, he shall be fined in part. That is, whether it is formed or not, which the wise say happens within the space of forty days." These, then, are the words of the teachers, Syrian and Greek, I mean. The Syrians say that the body is formed first and the soul is created in it afterward from nothing. The Greeks say that the body is formed and the soul created in it from nothing at once and equally, so that neither of them comes before the other nor after the other, but both run together to union equally and at once, the body being formed from seed and the soul from nothing. We agree with these Greek teachers, who say that the body is formed and the soul created in it at once and equally. We hold to them and add ourselves to their correct view. We will also give demonstrations that this opinion is true. First we will speak against those who said that the soul precedes the body in its creation. Not only did the ancient pagans say this, but also some in our own time who are called Christians, though they are heretics. These people claim to show from three arguments that the soul precedes the body in its creation. Their first argument is this. Moses, they say, said that God created this creation in six days and completed it on the sixth day, and from that day onward He created nothing. If what they said is true, that God completed on the sixth day all the works He had made, and nothing else came after the completion, then clearly He did not create souls after that sixth day. Therefore souls were created beforehand, before bodies. We answer this argument of theirs as follows. When Moses said that God completed on the sixth day all the works He had made, he meant that He completed all the creatures He had created on that

sixth day, and from then on He did not create any other creature that had not already been created by Him in the six days. If the souls He creates each day were new creatures, not created in the six days, then Moses' statement that God completed on the sixth day the works He had made would be false. But the souls He creates each day are not new creatures, since on that very sixth day He created the soul of Adam and the soul of Eve, which are equal in nature to the souls He creates each day. Because He created them on that very sixth day, Moses' statement is confirmed and true: God completed on the sixth day the works He had made, in that after that sixth day He did not create any new creature that had not already been created. And what we say is also true, that He creates souls continually every day, because they are not a kind of creature that was not created in the six days. Therefore souls do not precede bodies in their creation. Again, that God creates souls every day is true from the words of Zechariah the prophet, who said, "who forms the spirit of man within him." By saying "who forms," he made known that He continually forms the spirits of human beings. Again, it is known that He creates souls every day from the words of the Lord, who said, "My Father is working until now,

and I too am working." By saying "I am working" He made known three meanings. The first is that He creates souls continually. The second is that He takes care of His creatures and governs them in winter and summer, in sowing and harvest, in the rains He sends down and the rivers He makes flow, in striking and killing, and so on. The third is that He preserves them so that they do not perish. Their second argument is this. In the beginning, they say, God created creation from nothing, but today He creates creatures from something: a human being from a human being, a horse from a horse, [?] from [?], and so on. If in the beginning He created creatures from nothing and today creates them from something, and souls belong to the creatures created from nothing, then they were created in the beginning and precede bodies in their creation. [Our answer is] that God did not create all the creatures of the beginning from nothing. Some He created from nothing and some from something. Those He created from nothing are earth, water, air and fire, and souls. Those He created from something are the firmament, birds, creeping things, cattle, trees, grass, and the rest. We learn these things from the holy Scripture of the blessed Moses. So in the beginning He created some creatures from nothing and some

from something. And here is the precise reckoning: just as in the beginning He created some creatures from nothing and some from something, so too today He creates some creatures from nothing, by which I mean souls, and some from something, by which I mean the bodies of human beings and of irrational animals, and so on. Their third argument is this. A human being is composed of the four elements and of a rational soul. Just as the elements come first and exist before a human being is composed, so too the soul comes before the body, they say. The answer: your demonstration does not fit, namely that the rational soul comes before the composition of a human being just as the elements do. A human being is composed of a body made of the four elements and of a rational soul. So we must conclude as follows: just as the body does not come before the composition of a human being, neither does the rational soul. A human being is composed of a body made of the four elements and of a rational soul. So we must conclude as follows: just as the body does not come before the composition of a human being, neither does the rational soul come before its composition. So this demonstration supports our argument, not yours. Therefore the soul does not precede the body in its creation. We say to them again: if the soul had come first and been created before the body, it ought to remember, from before

it came to the body, what it was like and what state it was placed in. For it has memory, and memory is one of its natural powers. Yet we see and observe that it remembers nothing of the kind. Therefore the soul does not precede the body in creation. We say again that if it had come first and only afterward come to the body and been united with it, one of two things would have happened. Either it would not have entered the body at all, seeing its own rationality and the glory of its nature, and the lowliness and baseness of the body's nature. Or it would have entered by force, and would feel toward the body not love and harmony but hatred and division. Yet we see that it loves the body, is in harmony with it, and is drawn very strongly to its desires. These things make it known that the soul does not precede the body in its creation. Then there are those who say that the body is formed first and the soul created in it afterward. They too try to establish this opinion of theirs with demonstrations. That this is true, they say, is known from the fact that the law did not decree a sentence of death on someone who strikes a woman and makes her miscarry before the infant has been formed in shape and members. This is because the soul is not united with it while it has not yet been formed in shape

and members, and so the law did not decree a sentence of death for it. [We answer that] this was not the reason, for the soul was united with it at the emission of the seed. The reason is that the miscarried body, not yet formed in shape and members, is not distinguished from irrational animals, so there is no sentence of death for it. Once it has been formed in shape and members, and is thereby distinguished from irrational animals, the law decreed a sentence of death on whoever destroyed it. That this is so is known from the fact that killing reaches the body and not the soul, according to the word of the Lord who said, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." Therefore the body does not precede the soul in its formation. Their second demonstration is this. That the body precedes the soul in formation, they say, is known from what the blessed Moses said about God: that He first formed dust, and afterward breathed into it the breath of life. We say to them that the prophet Moses was telling divine matters in human words. In fact, God there formed the dust, created the soul and breathed into it all at once, in a way beyond our understanding, mind and speech. And when Moses wanted to bring this divine and swift matter

into human words, he could not say everything at once, in a single word, as befitted that swift act. So he was compelled to say that He formed dust and then breathed a soul into it. But someone may object: "If that is so, Moses should have said that God formed the dust and breathed a soul into it at once and equally." We answer him that if he had spoken that way, he would have been made an interpreter and not a writer. Moses is the writer of Scripture, not its interpreter. The task of the writer is only to write that God formed dust from the earth and breathed a soul into it. Which of them came first or later, or whether both were created equally at once, these questions and others like them are for interpreters to discuss, not for writers. This is what we say against those who claim that the body precedes the soul in its formation. We, however, say this: the soul does not precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. Rather, at once, with the emission of the seed, the soul too is created from nothing in that very moment and is united with it. That this is so is shown by these demonstrations. Every beginning is the beginning of an end,

and whatever belongs to the beginning belongs to the end. The essence of a human being is one, composed of soul and body. And the essence of a human being is given both to the human being's beginning and to his end. So just as the end of a human being is soul and body, his beginning must also be soul and body. Therefore the soul does not precede the body, nor the body the soul. Suppose the beginning of a human being were seed alone, without a rational soul with it, while at the end of a human being body and soul are separated from each other. Then the essence of a human being would not be given equally to his beginning and his end, but with addition and diminution: diminution at his beginning and addition at his end. And if the rational and incorporeal soul is not present at the emission of the seed, while a human being is composed of soul and body, that is, of the corporeal and the incorporeal, then this beginning is not that of a human being but of a non-human. So there would be a time when a human being is a non-human, and when the soul entered him he became a human being. Socrates, or anyone else, would then turn out to be at one time

a human being and at another time not a human being, which is false and loathsome. The book of Job, the victorious among the righteous, also testifies that the body is formed and the soul created in it at once. For it says: "Did you take clay of the earth, and form a rational living being, and set it on the earth?" By saying "form a rational living being," it shows that soul and body are formed without separation. These things show, therefore, that the soul does not precede the body, nor the body the soul. Rather, at once and equally, the body is formed from seed and the soul is created from nothing by the Creator of all, who is God and who is able to do whatever He wills. An inquiry into whether a soul is united with human seed every time it is emitted, or not. We have already said that the soul does not precede the body, nor the body the soul, but that both come together equally, the soul being created from nothing together with what is formed from seed. So the questioner asks: every time a man alone emits human seed, is a soul created from nothing and united with it? We say no. Every time a man alone emits seed, or a woman alone, or the two seeds happen to be emitted for some reason, nothing comes of them

conception, then the soul is not created at all, nor is it united to it. The soul is created and united only when these three conditions are fulfilled: first, that both seeds are emitted into the womb; second, that they unite with each other; third, that they bind together with one another so that the body may be formed and composed from them. Then the soul is created; the soul is created and united to the body. But if these three conditions are not fulfilled with respect to the seed, the soul is neither created nor united with them, because they are not fit to receive it. For the completion of the human body comes from both seeds. This is known from the fact that sometimes a male is conceived and sometimes a female, according as one of them prevails over the other. As some of the physicians say, when the man's seed prevails a male is conceived, and when the woman's prevails a female is conceived. Therefore, when these three conditions are fulfilled with respect to the seed of both, the soul is created and united to them at the Creator's command. Chapter showing for what reason the souls of infants do not distinguish good from evil and truth from falsehood. For what reason do the souls of infants and of small children not distinguish good from evil

and truth from falsehood? Is it because they are inferior in their nature, or in their natural powers, to the souls of youths and of men? We say no. These souls are not inferior in their natures to other souls, nor do they lack any of the natural powers, for they are equally rational, perceptive [?], intellective, knowing, and so on. It is rather because the members of infants' bodies are deficient and undeveloped, incomplete and unfit to receive the power of the soul so that it may act in them. They therefore remain unable to display its power, by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood or good from evil. For by its nature the soul is able to discern these things. But because the members of the body, which are its instruments, are deficient, incomplete and unfit to receive its power, its discernment, by which it distinguishes good from evil or truth from falsehood, is not displayed. A scribe does not write with a reed pen that has not been cut and is not finished, yet no one says that he does not know how to write. With a lyre that has not been tuned and is not finished the lyre-player does not play, though he is skilled at playing. And likewise with … with wood that is not

prepared, not finished and not suitable, the carpenter does no carpentry, though he knows how to, and no one says that he does not know how. In the same way the soul of infants does not distinguish truth from falsehood, or good from evil, in the incomplete members of their bodies, because those members are not suitable, although by nature it is able to distinguish good and evil, truth and falsehood. It has this ability [?], but the members of the body move it without bringing it into action, because they lack completion and are not suitable. Chapter showing where the soul is: outside the body, inside the body, or both outside and inside the body. Some people make this division concerning the soul: the soul, they say, is either outside the body, or inside and outside; the soul is either outside the body, or inside the body, or inside and outside. They make this division to press the hearer into falling into one of its three branches. Some say that it is outside the body. We say that this is not true. For if it were outside the body, thoughts would not move within it.

Others say that it is inside the body. We say that this too is simply not true. For if it were inside the body, the outer members of the body would be deprived of it. The soul dwells in the whole body, and there is not a single part of the body bare of it or of its life. Others say it is inside and outside the body. We say that this too is not true. For if it were inside and outside the body, it would be divisible, like air, which is both inside and outside the body. Therefore the soul is not said to be outside the body, nor inside the body, nor inside and outside. Rather, we say that it is in the whole body, united with it. Chapter showing whether the soul is united to all the members of the body or to one of them. It is right to investigate here whether it is united and interwoven with all of them, or with one member only. Some of the physicians say that it is united with the brain and dwells in it, and that this is known from the fact that when the brain is injured, the operations of the soul, which are rational, are impaired. Others say that it is united with the heart and dwells in it, and that this is known from the fact that thoughts and reflections move in it. We say that both these opinions are false. This is known from the fact that, if it were so, a human being would be composed of soul and brain alone, or of soul and heart alone, and not of soul and body. But the claim that a human being is composed of brain alone and soul is false, and so is the claim that he is composed of soul and heart alone. Therefore both these views are false. We, however, say that the soul is united to the whole body, and that there is not a single member in it, small or great, bare of it and of its life; rather, it is united to the whole body. That this is so is known from the fact that a human being is composed of body and soul. Chapter investigating whether, when the soul changes from good to evil and from love to hatred, it is its nature that changes and alters, or its will. Someone asks here: when the soul changes from good to evil, and from love to

hatred, and from righteousness to iniquity, and to all the other opposites of this kind, is it its nature that changes, or its will? We say that the nature of the soul does not change at all, and this is known from the following. The nature of the soul is life, as we said above, and immortality and incorporeality, and its natural powers are perception, rationality and the rest, which we set out above. It is known, then, that the nature of the soul does not change, nor its power in life, from the fact that it does not go from living to non-living, nor does it change from immortality to mortality, or from spiritual to corporeal, and it does not change from perception to rationality [?]. Therefore the nature of the soul does not change so that instead of living it becomes non-living, instead of spiritual corporeal, instead of immortal mortal, and instead of rational irrational and without perception. Rather, it is its will that changes from good to evil, from obedience to disobedience, from love to hatred, from righteousness to iniquity, and so on. Chapter showing

how these three differ from one another: mind, I mean, and spirit and soul. Are mind, spirit and soul three, or two, or one? And if they are three, or two, in what do they differ from one another? We say that Apollinaris, who was bishop of Laodicea, said that the mind is other than the soul. For this he was anathematized, he and his doctrine, since he went on to build other things upon this according to his [?]. Aristotle said that the mind is that which in potentiality is established in a human being together with him, while that which is in actuality enters from outside, not to complete the being of a human being, but toward the advancement of knowledge of the theories of natures; hence all people who have mind in actuality are so called [?]. Plato did not say that a human being consists of body and soul, but that he is a soul using a body. Others say that the mind is like this: just as the eye is in the body, so the mind is the eye of the soul, that is, its power of sight. And others thought and spoke otherwise. We, however, say that soul, spirit and mind are one and the same, and all three are one thing.

For these are three names that signify one nature and one definite hypostasis. That soul, spirit and mind are one and the same is known from these proofs. (1) If it were not so, a human being would be found to be composed of four natures: of soul, I mean, and of mind, of spirit and of body. (2) If it were not so, these three, soul, I mean, and mind and spirit, would be found to be three hypostases and three natures of ours. Which of them acts in the body and which does not? Or do all three act? And which of the three is repaid according to its works and which is not? Are all three repaid? These, then, are shameful notions and great absurdities. (3) That these three are all one is known from the fact that the divine Scripture says they are one, and calls the soul mind and the mind soul, and the soul spirit and the spirit soul. David, the singer of divine songs, says of man: His spirit goes forth, and he returns to his dust. And Solomon his son says: The body returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to the Lord who gave it. And the prophet Zechariah says: He forms the spirit of man within him.

Isaiah too says: My soul has longed for you even in the night; my spirit seeks you early. See how all of these named the soul spirit and called the spirit soul. From Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, from the commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: "What then, is Adam dust alone? Or did he also have another substance, akin to the beings above and incorporeal, which Scripture calls soul and spirit? It is known to everyone that he had this too. Akin to the beings above and incorporeal, which Scripture calls soul and spirit: it is known to everyone that he had this too." This holy and chosen teacher too says that Scripture calls this one and the same substance both soul and spirit. Saint Gregory the Theologian also, in the oration on the Nativity, calls the soul spirit when he says of man that he is "spirit, earthly and heavenly, temporal and immortal, visible and intelligible, midway between greatness and lowliness; the same both spirit and flesh: spirit because of grace, flesh because of pride." You see how he named the soul spirit. Therefore soul, spirit and mind are one nature of ours. Chapter showing that the soul, when

it is released from the body, does not perish but is preserved, or subsists in its own subsistence. When, then, the soul is released from the body to which it is bound and is separated from it, it does not perish, but is preserved, or subsists individually in its own subsistence. That this is so is known from these proofs. (1) Everything that exists subsists either by itself or in another. Whatever subsists in another, not possessing a subsistence of its own, [?] that thing in which it subsists and turns constantly toward it, because its nature is preserved in the other's subsistence; and if that other is destroyed, it too perishes. Now the soul, while it is in the body, often hands the body over of its own will to tortures and to death, so that the body may be released and destroyed. And it does this to the body when it judges that this benefits it. For if it had no subsistence of its own once separated from the body, it would not hand it over to perish, since it would know that when the body perished it too would perish. But because it gives the body over to die and be destroyed, we know that when it is separated from it, the soul possesses a subsistence of its own, subsists by itself, and has its own hypostasis. (2) That it subsists in its own subsistence after it is separated is known from the fact that it is a substance, as we showed earlier in the theories above. And a substance subsists

by itself, without needing another in which to subsist. (3) The body is the instrument of the soul, because through it the soul does good and evil; and whoever works with an instrument is not destroyed when he throws his instrument away. Just as a carpenter is not destroyed when he throws away his wood and his saw, but is preserved and endures, and as an architect is not destroyed when he throws away his [?], but is preserved and endures, so too the soul, when it is separated from the body, which is its instrument, does not perish and is not destroyed, but is preserved and endures. Therefore we are one thing, what is ours is another, and the things belonging to what is ours are yet another. We are the soul; ours is the body; and the things belonging to what is ours are possessions. Philosophy cares for us; medicine cares for what is ours; and the trades of every kind care for the things belonging to what is ours. Things that are cared for by different arts have different substances. Therefore, as a substance, the soul is a substance distinct from the substance of the body, and when it is separated it is preserved by itself. (4) That it is preserved and endures after it is separated from the body is known from the fact that it is immortal, as we showed in the sixteenth chapter. And what is immortal

never perishes, but is preserved and endures, whether united with another or separated from it. (5) The holy Scriptures testify that the soul is preserved and endures after it is released from the body. God said to Moses: I am the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob. And God is not the God of the dead but of the living. By saying "not of the dead but of the living," he showed that their souls live and are preserved and endure. And Solomon said: The dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit turns back to the Lord. He showed that the soul is preserved, lives and endures. And the Lord said in the Gospel: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. By saying that the soul is not killed he showed two things: first, that the soul is incorporeal, since it does not undergo bodily sufferings; second, that it is immortal; and what is immortal is preserved and subsists, neither perishing nor being destroyed. And again he said, in the story about Lazarus, that after the rich man died and was buried, the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham's bosom, and the rich man asked Abraham for water. By saying, then, that the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham's bosom, and by the reply

to the rich man, by all these things he showed that souls, when released from bodies, live and are preserved and endure in their own hypostases. Again, Paul says of himself that he was caught up to the third heaven, and he added: Whether in the body or without the body, I do not know. If his soul was caught up without his body, as he says, it is clear that after the soul is separated from the body it endures and is preserved, just as the Apostle's soul was separated from his body while being preserved. Again, he wrote to the Hebrews: Remember those who are afflicted, as people who are yourselves clothed in flesh. If, then, the one who wears is one thing and what is worn is another, it is clear that the nature of the soul is one thing and the nature of the body that clothes it is another. And just as someone who wears a garment lives, is preserved and endures after he has taken it off, so too the soul is preserved and endures after it has taken off the body, its garment. Chapter showing that after the soul is separated from the body its knowledge, its perception and its memory are preserved, and that it therefore knows, perceives and remembers after it is separated from the body. First it is right to investigate who those are who say that its knowledge is not preserved after it is separated from the body. Then we shall set out

their arguments on this and the solutions to them, and then we shall show our own glory [?]. We say that it is the Nestorians, and some others with them, who say that the knowledge of the soul is not preserved after it is separated from the body, and that it therefore neither knows nor remembers. They try to show this through the following arguments. Their first argument is this: If, they say, the knowledge of souls is preserved after they are separated from bodies, the souls of the righteous know that they did good and therefore rejoice, while those of the wicked know that they did evil and are therefore distressed; and joy and distress are delight and torment. In that case the justice of God is not seen, since souls did good and evil together with bodies, yet the souls are delighted and tormented without the bodies with which they did good and evil. We, however, resolve this argument of theirs as follows. We say that joy and distress are not the kingdom and Gehenna, nor are they delight and torment. For the joy and distress that come about on account of the deed for which they arise are [?]

Take an illustration of this. There were those two servants of Pharaoh who were imprisoned in the prison with Joseph. To one of them Joseph said, "After three days Pharaoh will restore you to your service," and to the other he said, "After three days Pharaoh will kill you." Therefore from that time the one began to rejoice greatly, while the other was greatly distressed. The joy of the one was over his service to Pharaoh, and as for the distress of the other, it was not the killing, but distress on account of his killing. Again, if a king said to two of his servants, to one, "Tomorrow I will give you a hundred thousand denarii," and to the other, "I will kill you," the one would rejoice and the other would be distressed. The joy of the one would not be called the hundred thousand denarii, nor would the distress of the other be the killing; it would be distress on account of the killing. In the same way, the joy with which the souls of the righteous rejoice after they are separated from bodies is not the kingdom and delight, nor is the distress with which the souls of the wicked are distressed [the torment]. (1) Again we say this: joy and distress on account of a deed are as distinct from it as potentiality is distinct from actuality. Just as we say

that a child is a carpenter in potentiality but not a carpenter in actuality, so neither are joy and distress on account of a deed the same thing as the deed itself; they are different things. (2) Again: the delight that is in the kingdom of heaven no eye of flesh has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the heart of man, as it is written; and so too the torment that is in Gehenna. But joy and distress, even though the eye of flesh has not seen them, because they are accidents, the ear of flesh has heard of them, and they have entered the heart of man. Therefore the joy and distress that attach to the souls of human beings after they are separated from the body are not the delight of the kingdom and the torment of Gehenna, as these people say. Their second argument is this: The soul, they say, has by its nature knowledge, perception and memory while it is united with the body. Therefore, when it is released from the body, it does not have these natural things until it is joined again to the body. Just as fire that is joined to matter heats and gives light, heat and luminosity being natural to it; and therefore, when it is released from matter, it does not heat

or give light until it is joined again to matter. So too, they say, the soul neither knows nor perceives nor remembers after it is released from the body, until it is joined again to the body. Solution: The fire that you brought as an illustration does not lose, when it is released from matter, the heat and luminosity that it possessed by nature; rather, these qualities are preserved in the fire itself, even though they are not visible to you. In the same way, the harmony of the body is not preserved, because the body is dissolved, but these things are preserved by nature in the soul, even though they are not displayed in the body. Just as when an instrument is damaged in the hand, the art is not damaged along with it in what it possesses by nature: the lyre-player's skill is not cut off, nor does his voice perish, if a string of the lyre is cut; nor is the carpenter's finger cut off if his saw and his wood are broken. So too the soul does not lose what it possesses by nature because it is released from the body. These, then, are their arguments and our solution. But it is right first to distinguish in what the soul's knowledge differs from its perception, from its recollection and from its memory. And when we have distinguished these four from one another, then

we shall show that the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved after it is released from the body, and that it therefore knows and remembers. Knowledge, then, is that by which the soul knows divine and human things, and by which it knows good and evil matters, beneficial and harmful ones, and so on. In short, the soul's knowledge is the power by which it knows things. The soul's perception is not something other than its knowledge, but is the same as its knowledge. This is shown as follows: the body, when something cold or hot or sweet or sour or the like touches it, perceives it, because there is in it a soul, which is other than the body and possesses knowledge, so that its perception, though seemingly other, is the same as its knowledge [?]. For the soul's perceiving a thing is nothing other than its knowing things. Therefore the soul's perception is the same as its knowledge, and its knowledge the same as its perception. Let us now show how memory differs from recollection. First we say that things are done in three ways: some in past time, some in present time, and some again

in future time. Memory, then, is that which gathers and keeps the knowledge and learning of things that were done in past time. This is known from the fact that no one says, "I remember what I see and hear," nor, "I remember what is going to happen," but rather, "I remember what is past." Things in present time we perceive and know through sense and knowledge: if they are perceptible, we perceive them through the senses of the body; if they are intelligible, we know them through the knowledge of the soul. Future things we place [?] through hope and expectation, for no one knows what is going to happen unless the gift of prophecy has been given him by God. Does one not say, "I expect and declare that there will be [?]," or "there will not be"? Memory, therefore, is that which gathers and keeps the learning of past time. Recollection, on the other hand, is that which is preceded by forgetting. That is why we say that it is memory that the soul has after it is released from the body. Is not recollection, then, said of the soul while it is joined with the body? For forgetting comes about because of the mixture of the body. Memory, however,

belongs to the soul both while it is joined with the body, and when it is being released from it, and after it has been released from it. It is right again to show how some came to say that the soul's memory ceases after it is released from the body. We say: was it not because its recollection ceases, and, supposing memory to be recollection, they said that memory ceases? We, however, say that these differ greatly from each other. For just as forgetting is a passion of the body, and recollection is bound up with forgetting, so recollection too is a passion of the body; but memory is a natural affection of the soul, and therefore it does not cease from the soul when it is released from the body. Now that these things have been distinguished and clearly shown, [we turn to show] that after the soul is separated from the body its knowledge and memory are preserved, and that it therefore knows and remembers. That this is so is known from these proofs. First, of the powers of the soul some are natural and some are accidental. The natural ones are perception, thought, knowledge, rationality, volition [?], memory and the like. The accidental ones are anger, desire, the sensation of the five senses, imagination, and things like these, as we showed in the tenth chapter. When, then, the soul is separated from the body, the accidental powers

cease from it without delay, because they came to it on account of the body. But the natural powers never cease from it after it is released from the body. This is known from two things: first, from the fact that they are planted in it by nature; and second, from the fact that if these natural powers ceased from it, its nature would cease. For its nature, which is life, is not something other apart from these powers, nor are these powers something other apart from its nature. It is not a body, such that its natural powers could be apart from its nature; rather, it is spiritual and incorporeal. Therefore its nature is to live, to perceive, to think, to know, to reason, to move of itself, and to remember. Therefore the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved after it is separated from the body. Second: we say that the wise say that rationality has two kinds, one that gathers knowledge and another that holds what has been gathered. The one that gathers they called reflection, and this one that holds they named memory. Rationality is a power of the soul, and both while it dwells in the body and when it departs from it, it has this power. And rationality has these two powers, the gathering one, I mean, and the holding one. Therefore, when the soul is separated from the body, it reflects on and remembers what it did

here. Third, there is the reduction to absurdity. If the soul has no knowledge and memory after it is separated, then it is not right to hold the commemoration of the departed that the canons of the apostles command us. Paul commanded in his canon as follows: that the commemoration of those who have fallen asleep be performed on the third day, because on the third day our Lord rose from the tomb; on the ninth day, for the remembrance of the living and of those who have fallen asleep; and on the thirtieth day, according to the old law, for the Hebrews mourned [?] Moses for thirty days. If the soul has no knowledge and memory after it is separated from the body, then it is superfluous and useless for the deacon to proclaim at the offering, at the time of the holy mysteries, that those who have fallen asleep before us be remembered. But the soul's knowledge and its memories are preserved after it is released from the body. It would not be right for us who are Christians to ask the souls of the martyrs and saints to pray to God for us, if the soul's memory and knowledge were not preserved after it is released from the body. Are the souls of the holy believers and the souls of the wicked and [?] carried to one place and one abode until the day of resurrection? For if they neither know nor discern, it is all the same to them

whether they abide and are kept in one place or in many places, in bright places or in dark places. But if the souls of the saints and of the wicked are carried to separate places, the former to bright abodes and to be with the angels, the latter to the dark abode and to be with the demons, it is clear that the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved. Therefore, so that these absurdities may not be incurred [?], it is clear and evident that souls have knowledge and memory after they are released from bodies, and that they therefore know and remember. Fourth: this is known from the testimony of the holy Scriptures. Our Lord said in the Gospel, in the story about the rich man and Lazarus: Lazarus died, and the angels carried him to Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died and was buried, and while he was being tormented in Sheol he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he raised his voice and said, "Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame." He said to him, "My son, remember that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus his evil things. And besides all this, a great chasm stands between us, so that those

who wish to cross from you to us cannot, nor can anyone cross from us to you." He said to him, "I beg you to send him to my father's house, for I have five brothers; let him go and testify to them, so that they too may not come to this place of torment," and so on. By saying that the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham's bosom he showed two things: first, that the soul subsists in its own subsistence after it is released from the body; second, that angels carry the souls of the saints. When he says that the rich man lifted up his eyes, this is will, which belongs to the soul; therefore its will is preserved. When he says that he saw Abraham, this is knowledge. When he cried out and said, "Father Abraham, have mercy on me," it is clear that this belongs to the soul; therefore rationality is preserved. For the apostle Paul says: My life is Christ, and if I die, it is gain to me. Here [?] the Apostle compares his life here with the life after death, and says that if his soul, while it dwelt in his body, knew, understood and remembered, but after it was released from the body, or after he died, his soul did not know, understand or remember, this would be loss and harm to it. And just as

then, "If I die, it is gain to me"? And if the soul knew, understood and remembered after it was separated from the body just as it did while it dwelt in the body, how could he say, "It is gain to me if I die"? That would be loss, not gain. But it is known and evident that after the soul is released from its body and dies, it knows and understands more, and thinks and remembers more. This follows from his saying, "If I die, it is gain to me." Therefore, when the soul is released from the body, it knows, understands and remembers more than when it was in the body. An inquirer [?] asks: Just as the body sees with the eyes, hears with the ear and acts in other ways with its other members, does the soul likewise see with one part, and hear and know with another, or is this otherwise with it? Someone asks and inquires, saying: Just as the body sees with the eyes, hears with the ear, smells with the nostrils and acts in other ways with its other members, does the soul likewise see with one part, hear with another, and know and understand with another, or is this otherwise with it? First we will examine why the body sees only with the eyes and not with the whole of itself, and why

it hears only with the ear, and why it smells only with the nostrils and not with the whole of itself. After that we will speak about the soul, and how it hears, sees, understands and knows with the whole of itself. The body, then, sees only with the eyes because they have a kinship with the light of the sun, since their make-up differs in some way from that of the rest of the body. The eye is pure, clear, bright, gleaming and radiant, and through these qualities it has a kinship with the light of the sun, because the light of the sun is pure, clear, bright, gleaming and radiant. So when the light of the sun rests upon the eye, it enables it to see, because of the kinship the eye has with it. In the same way, those who dig pits in the earth, when they are cut off from the light of the sun and darkness reigns over them, bring a bronze mirror that gleams brightly and set it beneath the opening of the pits. Then the mirror receives the light of the sun from above, because of the kinship that bronze has with light, being clear, pure and very radiant, and the mirror reflects that light and so sends it this way and that until it lights up those who are digging the earth. So too with

pure, gleaming silver, and with water that is pure, clear and radiant: when the light of the sun falls on them, they pass on a bright gleam, which falls on whatever wall is nearby. It is therefore known that the eye alone of the whole body sees, because it has a kinship with the light of the sun. The ears, for their part, are the only things that hear, while the rest of the body does not, because their openings are pierced from the outside right through to the brain, with nothing in between. When the air is stirred, it carries [?] the sound, and nothing hinders it until it brings it into the opening of the ears; it strikes the brain, and the brain perceives it.
