So too the nostril, for another reason, is the only thing that smells, and not the whole body as well. The body, then, because it is composed of different and many members, does not see with the whole of itself, nor hear or smell with the whole of itself. Rather, it sees with one part, hears with another, smells with another, and acts and feels in other ways with yet another. The soul, however, is not like this: it sees with the whole of itself, hears with the whole of itself, and understands and knows with the whole of itself. And it is known that it is so because it is

simple and spiritual. Being simple and spiritual, it is not composed of members. It therefore has no members with which it sees, others with which it hears, and others with which it knows; rather, it understands with the whole of itself and knows with the whole of itself. The angels too are like this: each one of them sees with the whole of himself, hears with the whole of himself and knows with the whole of himself. Therefore the soul, when it is separated from the body, sees with the whole of itself, hears with the whole of itself, knows and understands with the whole of itself, and perceives and remembers with the whole of itself, because it is spiritual, incorporeal, simple and uncompounded. On what the soul knows and what it does not know when it is separated from the body. When the soul is separated from the body, it understands and knows the following. It knows itself. It knows that it is made and has a Maker. It knows that it was in the body and has departed from it. It knows that it will take up its body again on the day of the resurrection. It knows the angels and the demons when they gather at its departure from the body. It knows the souls among which it will be until the resurrection. It knows what it did here, whether good or evil. It knows the one who keeps it,

and whether it is in delight or in torment. It knows and also perceives the offerings that are offered on its behalf. These things and things like them the soul knows after it is released from the body. And it is known that this is so because it retains its knowledge, its perception, its understanding, its memory and the rest of its natural powers after it has departed from the body. But there are other things which the soul does not know after it is released from the body. It does not know what we do here after it has departed, nor whether times are good or bad among us. Nor does it know the chastisements that are sent upon us from God, nor the things that are far from it. These the soul does not know after it has departed from the body, nor things like them. And it is known that this is so because the soul is limited, and therefore its knowledge is necessarily limited as well. For one whose being is unlimited has unlimited knowledge too, while one whose being is limited has limited knowledge too. Thus God, whose being is unlimited, has unlimited knowledge as well; but angels and souls, whose natures are limited, have limited knowledge too. And if the soul's knowledge is limited, just as its nature is limited,

then after it has departed from the body it does not know what we do here, nor the things in this world, nor the things far from it — unless this knowledge is given to it from God as a gift, just as he gave prophecy to the prophets, and they saw beforehand things to come and things far away with the eyes of prophecy and spoke of them. So if this knowledge is given to the soul as a gift from God, who is able to do all things, it knows. The other kinds of knowledge we spoke of above, however, it knows truly and properly, because its natural powers, by which it knows them, are preserved. On those who gather and assemble around the soul when it is released from the body. We say that angels and demons gather and assemble around it and meet it. And why do they gather around it and meet it? We say that the angels gather around it because they want it to go with them, and so they recount its good deeds. Likewise the demons gather around it because they want it to go with them, and so they recount its evil deeds. That angels and demons gather and assemble around the soul when it is separated from the body

and meet it is known from these true testimonies. The Lord said in the Gospel to those who did not feed him or care for him through the poor: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire that is prepared for the devil and his angels." And again, in the account of the rich man and Lazarus, he said that when Lazarus died the angels carried him to Abraham's bosom. Jude the apostle too, in the Catholic Epistle, speaks of the dispute Satan had when he contended with Michael the angel over the burial of Moses: "Michael the archangel, when he was speaking with the devil and disputing over the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a reviling judgment against him, but said, 'May the Lord rebuke you.'" It is known also from the account of Antony the solitary, which Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and the holy Mar Severus of Antioch relate as follows: Once, when Antony was about to eat bread, he rose to pray at the ninth hour and perceived

that his mind was lifted up, and he thought he was outside his body. He saw his soul being lifted up in the air and moving towards God, while gentle angels who loved mankind went before him and accompanied him. When he had gone part of the way, he saw others, hideous and bitter, who glared fiercely and terrifyingly. They came and stood to meet him in the air, set up toll-gates against him and tried to stop him from passing. They said to him, "We hold you, for you are as guilty as these who are ours." And when those demons wanted to bring up the deeds he had done since his birth, the angels who were accompanying him rebuked them, saying: "All his failings and sins from his birth until he became a monk the Lord has blotted out in his goodness. As for his conduct and his victories since he became a monk and pledged himself to God, you are henceforth powerless [?] to approach, and you have no ground at all for accusation." Then they all fled in confusion, and like smoke

they vanished. His way was set free and became unhindered, and so his soul was lifted up until it reached the place to which it was going. After this his mind gathered itself again, it seemed to him that he returned to his body, and he found himself wholly in his cell. Amazed in his mind, he gave thanks to God for what had happened, and he marveled greatly at how the evil powers deal with us — with the soul after it is separated from the body — and what bitter hatred they bear towards it. Because of this he forgot about food, though hunger was gnawing [?] within his belly. And love drew him on to learn exactly whether what he had seen was true or not. For this reason he afflicted his body with humility, and the old man wore out his body with excellent ways of life. Then one night Christ called him, saying, "Antony, go outside and see." When he went outside, he saw something in the likeness of a man standing in the midst of the earth, whose stature reached up to heaven. In his appearance

he was terrifying and repulsive, and his ugliness exceeded even his height. Around him he saw a great multitude flying up from the earth and rising on wings. Some of them flew up as far as his hands, and then fell and were thrust down. Others flew and rose above his arms and escaped from his grasp. Over those who flew and fell beneath him he greatly rejoiced and was delighted; but over those who rose above him he was greatly distressed and embittered, and he gnashed his teeth and raged. When Antony saw this vision, Christ declared to him, "Understand what is being shown to you." At once he understood that what was shown to him in the vision was the passage of souls. For the tall man was the devil, the ruler of the air and of the spirit, as the apostle Paul calls him. Those who flew and fell beneath him were those who

had become entangled in the snares of sin, struck down by the various kinds of wickedness and caught in his net. Those who flew and rose above him were those who had cast off from themselves the passions of the flesh and the earthly weight of sin, had escaped his traps and had flown to heaven by holy conduct. It is therefore known from these things that when the soul is separated from the body, angels and demons gather and assemble around it. Athanasius of Alexandria further relates [?] about the holy Antony that his zeal to strive and to humble himself grew greater in his old age. And so, when he was once on the mountain, he lifted his eyes to heaven and saw someone being drawn up. Fear and amazement fell upon him, and he called blessed the one who had been found worthy of this ascent, and he asked the Lord to make known to him who he was. And a voice was heard from heaven saying to him: "This is the soul of Amun, who lived in the region of Nitria." Now this man was holy and chosen, an excellent solitary from his youth to his old age, whose end surpassed

his beginning. From Nitria, the region where he lived, to the mountain where Antony lived was a journey of thirteen days, as they say. The holy teachers too testify that when the soul is separated from the body, angels and demons gather around it and meet it. Of the holy Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of the city of Athens, from the letter to Demophilus the monk: "One must know that those who have dared to do [?] such things against someone [?] did not begin with this, but from the time they first set about it [?]; and, contrary to this, to do good to someone, whatever they wished [?]. For they have made themselves the dwelling-place, in every way, either of divine virtue or of brutish passions. The virtuous become companions and associates of the angels, here and hereafter, and with them inherit a blessed eternity in that incorruptible world, and are with God forever and ever — which is greater and more excellent than all good things. But those others fall further and further away from their own divine peace, and here, and again after their death, they are gathered with the brutish demons." Therefore we ought to take great care to be with our Lord at all times, and not with the demons.

Of the holy Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from the discourse on martyrdom [?]: "Do you not know, my brothers, what fear, trembling and distress we will face when the soul is separated from the body? For there gather against it the opposing powers, the rulers of darkness who hold the world of wickedness, the principalities and dominions and the spirit of wickedness. And with trembling they then seize the soul, bringing against it all the sins it has committed, knowingly and unknowingly, from its youth until the time it was taken away, and they stand and accuse it of everything it has done. Then the powers of God come and stand facing those of the adversary, and they too recount its good deeds. So in what anguish do you think it is at that hour, until the verdict comes and it is set free?" Of the holy Severus, from the letter to Thomas, bishop of Germanicia: "For when the soul is separated from the body, after its departure from the body it is met by the angelic and good powers and by a band of evil demons, so that, according to the working of the deeds it has done, whether good or evil,

to the places that are fitting, either the one or the other receives it, to be kept until the last day, on which we shall all stand and be carried either to judgment or to eternal life, either to the flame of unquenchable fire or to the kingdom of heaven, which has no end." From the book of Isaiah, which he wrote about the joy that comes to the soul that wishes to serve God: "When the soul goes out of this world, angels go with it. Then the powers of darkness come out to meet it, wishing to seize it in order to examine whether they have anything of their own in it. At that point it is not the angels who fight with them; rather, the works it has done shelter it and guard it from them, so that they cannot come near it. If its works are pure, the angels rejoice before it until it meets God with joy. Then, in that hour, it forgets its work in this world and all its toil." Of the holy Mar Jacob, bishop of Edessa, from the discourse on the constitution of man: after the discussion of the tombs [?] and of human life in this world, and then of what death is, of the corruption in the grave, of the dissolution and separation of the body's members within the earth, and of the scattering of the bones to

Sheol, he says: "When the body is dissolved into dust according to God's sentence, and from there each of the elements passes back to its kin — water, air and fire — until in truth only dust is left, which goes to the earth, the dust that is its kin, the soul passes either to the souls of the righteous, or to the souls of the wicked together with the black, rebellious demons, according to the sentence that has gone out against it from God, until the time comes for the resurrection of the whole human race, and for the judgment and just recompense owed to each person according to his works and his conduct, or his deeds, here." See how the chosen and orthodox teachers have shown us clearly that when the soul is separated from the body, angels and demons assemble and gather around it and meet it: the angels bring forward its good deeds, because they want it to go with them, while the demons accuse it of its evil deeds, because they want it to go with them. Refuting those who say that souls circulate and pass from body to body, and showing their doctrine to be false. Some of

the pagans say that souls circulate and pass from body to body according to the good and evil they do. If a soul does good, it passes from the body in which it did good into another body that is better and finer than it; and if it does evil, it passes from that body into another body that is inferior and more loathsome than the one in which it did evil. We, however, say that what they say is false and abominable, and this is known from the following. (1) The soul knows and remembers, for knowledge and memory are its natural powers, as we showed in the chapters above. Therefore it knows the things it has done and also remembers them. If it circulated and passed from body to body, then when it passed into one of these bodies it would remember what it had done in the body from which it departed. Yet we know that the souls united to human bodies today do not remember being in other bodies, nor having done either good or evil in them. And if they object and say that knowledge and memory belong neither to the soul alone nor to the body alone, but to both together,

this objection has been answered for us in chapter thirty-three, which shows that the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved after it is separated from the body. (2) As for souls passing from bodies to bodies, one of two things must necessarily hold: either God transfers them, or they pass over by themselves. If God transfers them as a recompense for good and evil, he does not act justly, because the powers of the soul follow the temperament of the body; it is through the body that the soul performs good and evil. It would therefore be right for him to transfer, along with the souls, the bodily temperaments with which they performed good and evil. And if the souls pass from bodies to bodies by themselves, they do so either by nature or by will. If by nature, they ought all to pass to one place suited to them. If by will, they ought to pass into fine [?] and choice bodies, if their transfer lay in their own will. These are some of the natural proofs that show that souls do not pass from body to body. The testimonies from the holy Scriptures are these. The prophet David, singer of the priestly psalms [?], says: "My soul thirsts for you, O living God; when shall I come and see your face?"

His son Solomon says: "The body returns to the earth, and the spirit to the Lord who gave it." And our Lord said of Lazarus in the Gospel that he died and the angels carried him to Abraham's bosom. Stephen, the head and first of the martyrs, said as he was being stoned, "Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit." And the apostle Paul said, "I long to depart, so that I may be with Christ." It is therefore made known by all these that souls do not pass from bodies to bodies, nor circulate from body to body. Showing where souls are until the day of the resurrection. Someone asks: When human souls depart from their bodies, where are they until the resurrection? Some say that they are in this air between us and heaven, and remain in it until the day of the resurrection. But the holy Mar John of Constantinople rejects this view, and we with him. We say that it is not true, and that it is not true is known from the following proofs. (1) If souls are in this air after they are separated from their bodies, why do we say that there is another world? We would

no longer need another world if they are in this air. (2) That they are not in this air is known from the fact that the angels carried poor Lazarus to Abraham's bosom, as our Lord said; from the fact that the rich man asked to come and testify to his brothers and was not allowed; from the fact that when the other rich man wanted to pull down his barns, it was said to him, "This night your soul is required of you"; from David's saying to God, "When shall I come and see your face?"; and also from the apostle Paul's saying, "I long to depart, so that I may be with Christ." Therefore, when souls depart from bodies they are not in this air until the day of the resurrection, as these men have said. Others say that the souls of the upright, of the righteous, of the apostles, of the martyrs, of the saints and of others like them, when they depart from their bodies, mingle with the angels and are with them until the day of the resurrection; while the souls of the wicked and the unjust are with the demons and mingle with them until the day of the resurrection. We, for our part, say that this is true, and as a matter of fact and of time [?]

we confess and believe it. But this does not suffice to resolve and complete the question, since the question requires us to say where, and in what place, souls are when they are separated from their bodies, until the day of the resurrection. Others say that when souls are separated from their bodies they are not in a place, because they are spiritual and incorporeal, and what is spiritual and incorporeal has no need of a place to be in. Therefore, they say, souls are not in a place when they are separated from their bodies. First, then, we ought to speak about location and about place; after that we will speak about souls, whether or not they are in places when they are separated from their bodies. So let us say what location is. We say that the philosophers held many opinions about location. Some of them say that it is only length and breadth, and so it is not grasped by the senses but known by the mind. Others said that location is that which encloses the boundaries of a body. Others said that location is that which is between

the jar and the wine, and that which is between a body and the air — something intermediate, which is between the jar and the wine, between the water and the pitcher, and between a person's body and the air that surrounds it. Still others thought differently and said of location that it is not a place. [?] to gather together the views and opinions about location. So much, then, for what location is. Place, on the other hand, is a location bound up with a substance, such as the place where a person sits or sleeps. For we necessarily say that John stands in places, and that Socrates wrote in a place, by every means. These remarks about location and place are enough for now. Let us now inquire whether souls, when they depart from their bodies, need a location and a place to be in or not. We say that bodies need a location and a place to be in, because they are compounded and need length, height and breadth, and they also have boundaries. But the incorporeal, since it is not [?] and has neither length, depth nor breadth, needs neither location nor place.

But if this is so, someone might say, then those who said above that souls are not in a place when they are separated from their bodies are right. We say that "place" is used in two senses: a place suited for bodies to be in, and a place suited for the incorporeal to be in. For everything limited necessarily needs a place. The angels are therefore limited, and because they are limited they are necessarily in a place. The place suited to bodies is spoken of in ten ways: above, below, right, left, in front, behind, here, there, near and far. Every body is in one of these places. The place of souls, however, is none of these; rather, the place of souls is spiritual and wholly [?] subtle, suited for souls to be in. Therefore souls that are separated and departed from their bodies are necessarily in a place. Hence the question still remains: where, and in what place, does the soul remain until the resurrection? We say that the souls of the righteous, the upright and the saints are in the Paradise from which

Adam went out. The souls of the apostles, the martyrs and those excellent ones who are closest to God are above, beyond heaven. But the souls of the wicked and the unjust are in dark places beneath the earth until the resurrection. Others say that the souls of the wicked are in places of darkness until the resurrection, while those of the upright, the righteous, the apostles, the martyrs and the true believers who lived excellent lives are in Paradise until the resurrection, once they have departed from their bodies. This is known from the fact that God brought the soul of the thief there, saying to him, "Today you will be with me in Paradise." It is known, moreover, from the testimonies of [?] orthodox teachers on this point. Of the holy Gregory the Theologian, from the homily on Pascha: "At the time of the dispensation of the passion, the Godhead did not withdraw from either of the parts — for the gifts of God are irrevocable [?] — even though it separated the soul from the body by its own will. It remained with both of them. For it showed that the body did not receive corruption from death, and it loosed for it [?] the grip of death that held it;

and through the soul it prepared the way for the thief to the entrance of Paradise. Both things were accomplished together through the two, as the good Godhead was at work [?]: through the incorruptibility of the body it set the body free, and through the soul, its dwelling, the return of mankind to Paradise was being prepared." Of the holy Mar John, bishop of Constantinople, from the homily on why the tree from which Adam ate was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: "The thief entered Paradise, we say. And what of this? Are these, then, the good things that God has promised us? Do you not hear the divine Paul saying, 'Good things which the eye has not seen and the ear has not heard, and which have not entered the heart of man'? But Paradise the eye has seen, the ear has heard of by report, and the heart of man has conceived. For we have been speaking about such things, as you see, for many days now. How, then, has the thief's reward been paid? For God did not promise to bring us into Paradise, but into heaven itself; nor did he proclaim the kingdom of Paradise, but the kingdom of heaven. For he

began to preach and to say, 'Repent, for the kingdom has drawn near' — the kingdom of heaven, that is. If, then, he promised the kingdom of heaven, but brought the thief into Paradise, he has not yet paid him his reward." Of the holy Philoxenus of Mabbug: "For when our Lord was hanging on the cross for us, and two thieves were crucified with him, it is written that the thief on the right believed in him and said to him, 'Remember me, my Lord, when you come in your kingdom.' And Jesus at once promised him and said to him, 'Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.' A little while later he immediately led away the soul of the thief and, as he had promised him, took it with him to Paradise, where the souls of all the righteous were gathered around him [?]. And he taught [?] that bodily it would be preserved [?] in the tomb. And he went to the bodies that were in the tombs, and they thought that they had risen [?]. What [?]... and through his soul he visited the souls of the righteous and of sinners, some in Paradise and some in Sheol, and promised them the return to their bodies; and after other things [?]. For when

he went to Paradise and led the soul of the thief, who had been crowned on the cross, to be with him, he removed the cherub and the sharp edge of the sword that guarded Paradise, and he brought in with him the souls of all the righteous, which had been wandering outside, since the guards would not let them enter. And there, through his soul, he also proclaimed to them redemption and the return to their bodies. Not only did he remove the cherub; he also gathered them and brought them into Paradise, and by his word confirmed to them the resurrection of their bodies. From then until now, and on until the world comes to an end, the soul of every righteous person that departs from the body enters Paradise and dwells there until the time of his coming; but the souls of sinners are in Sheol." And concerning this the Scripture says that God went there, to Paradise, through his soul. Not only did the souls of the righteous enter in abundance, but, as I think, the angels as well. For if it is not written of the greatest of the angels that he entered, but only that he stood guard outside, how can we not confidently say that none of those other spiritual powers was permitted to enter there either? Showing

that the souls are mingled with these ranks and orders when they are separated from their bodies. When human souls are released from their bodies and depart from them, they are mingled with these orders and ranks until the resurrection. We say that the souls of the righteous, of apostles and martyrs, of prophets, of the just and of the holy, are with the angels when they depart from their bodies, and are mingled with them until the resurrection, because the angels dwell above heaven and also in Paradise. But when the souls of the wicked and the unjust are separated from their bodies, they are with the demons and are mingled with them until the resurrection. We know that this is so from the following proofs. First, it is clear from the principle of justice. Souls that, while they are in bodies in this world, follow an excellent way of life, one that resembles the angels and gives them rest, are mingled with the angels when they are released from their bodies, and they are with them, as something fitting for them and which they loved. But those souls which, while they dwelt [?] for them, and loved. But those souls which, while they dwelt in the body in this world, practised a way of life

that is evil and hateful, one that gives rest and gladness to the demons, are justly mingled with the demons when they are released from their bodies, and they are with them, as something fitting for them and which they loved. Second, it is also clear from this: when a soul is being released and is departing from the body, angels and demons gather and come to it. They assemble from two sides, facing each other, and each of them wants that soul to go with him, and they fight over it, as we show in chapter thirty-six. Of Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Athens, from the letter to Damphilus [?], a son of the covenant: It is right to know that those who try to walk [?] in someone, not from this; behold, from [?], and they thought toward him and toward receiving this, to do good to someone. For whatever they wanted in their soul they settled [?] from [?]. And it is concluded in chapter thirty-six, with the rest. [Chapter] that inquires which was created in the image of God: the soul, the body, or both of them together. And what is the image of God in which man was created, and the likeness? Which is in the image of God:

the soul, the body, or both of them together? We say: the soul alone. And this is clear from God. First: God is simple, incorporeal, incorruptible and immortal. Which of these two, then, is his image? The soul, which is simple, incorporeal, immortal and incorruptible, or the body, which is composite, corporeal, corruptible and mortal? Clearly it is the soul and not the body. Second: which is in the image of God? The body, which has the form of male and female, or the soul, which is above these things? Clearly it is the soul. Third: if the body, which is composed of elements, were the image of God, then the irrational animals would also be in the image of God, which is wicked and false. So these points make it known that the soul alone is in the image of God. Now it is right to inquire in what respect the soul is in the image of God. We say that the soul is in the image of God in these ways (and we say that in these ways): First: as God is without body, not corporeal, invisible and immortal, so too is the soul. Second: as God sees all things as Lord and in truth,

so too the soul sees all things, but in imagination and not in truth. Another: as God has authority over his creatures, so 'have dominion,' it says, 'over the fish of the sea and over the birds of heaven,' and the rest: he gave the soul freedom and authority over the household. Fourth: as God does all that he wills [?], so creatures serve man, bodily creatures and [?] creatures, and they praise God their Creator, whether they are corporeal or incorporeal. Fifth: man practises crafts, builds houses and creates as God does, which is found neither in the angels nor in the irrational animals. Sixth: he granted man to stand in his place in all this, like a servant who stands in his master's place in his city and in his house. Seventh: God performs mighty works and wonders, I mean raising the dead, cleansing lepers and opening the eyes of the blind, binding and loosing heaven, and the rest. God does these things by nature, but in his goodness he gave this to man as well, as a gift. As God is in his creation and works in it and governs it while he himself is not seen, so too the soul is in the body [?] and works

in it and governs it while it is not seen. Eighth: God said, 'Let us make man in our image,' that is, in the way in which God the Word was going to become incarnate and become a complete man without change. As the divine apostle said, 'The first man was dust from the earth, and the second man is the Lord from heaven.' Therefore, as man is composed of soul and body, one hypostasis and one composite nature, so too Christ, from divinity and humanity, is one hypostasis and one composite nature. As he too, the apostle Paul, said: 'As the children,' he says, 'share in flesh and blood,' so too God the Word shared in humanity. That is, what he said was this: as the soul of the children, together with flesh and blood, is one hypostasis and one composite nature, so too God the Word, together with ensouled [?] flesh, is one hypostasis and one composite nature. Ninth: God is three hypostases, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Spirit proceeding. In this image, then,

he also created three hypostases in mankind: I mean Adam, Eve and Seth. Adam, his creature, was unbegotten; Seth was begotten [?]; Eve proceeded. These are the ways in which man was created in the image of God. Let us now also inquire in what way man is the likeness of God, because it is written that God said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness.' We say that God is good, just, holy and merciful. So he made man by nature to resemble him in his goodness, his justice, his holiness and his mercy, as far as man is able to resemble him. In this way he will be good, just, holy and merciful, as our Lord said in the Gospel: 'Be merciful, as your Father in heaven is merciful.' Let us also inquire about the body, which is called the image of God, since it is called so by virtue of its union with the soul. Because of this union the soul gives to the body what is its own, and takes and receives what belongs to the body. For this reason, the union, the whole man is said to be in the image and likeness of God.

For the name 'man' denotes the compound of soul and body. That is why the blessed Moses also wrote: 'God said, Let us make men in our image and likeness.' As long as the soul is bound in the body and united with it, it grants the body to be called the image and likeness of God, by virtue of the union. But when it is released from the body, it no longer grants it this. Therefore the soul, of itself and in the proper sense, is the image and likeness of God, while the body is called the image and likeness of God by virtue of union, by participation and by borrowing.

Chapter showing that the departed benefit from the offerings that are offered on their behalf. Of Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis, a story he wrote about the solitaries: A man withdrew from this world. He had a wife, and also a daughter who died while she was still a catechumen. Her father distributed as alms to the poor the share that would have come to her, and her mother too never ceased entreating God for their daughter, who had departed from the world unbaptized. Then, while he was praying, a voice was heard by him: 'Your daughter has been baptized; do not grieve.' But he did not believe it. So the invisible voice spoke again:

'Dig up her grave.' He dug, and did not find her, for she had been moved and laid with the believers. Saint John of Constantinople, from the forty-first homily on the First Letter to the Corinthians: If those who have departed were sinners, then we should rejoice that they have been cut off from their sins and have not added to their wickedness, and you should help them as far as you can, not with tears but with prayers and supplications, with alms and offerings. For this was not devised idly, nor is it in vain that we commemorate those who have departed at the divine mysteries and offer on their behalf, asking the Lamb who lies there, who took away the sin of the world. It is so that some consolation may come to them from here. And it is not in vain that the one who stands at the altar, while the awesome mysteries are being celebrated, cries out for all who have fallen asleep in Christ and for those whose commemorations are being made. Otherwise commemorations would not be made on their behalf. For these rites of ours are not theatre, God forbid! They are performed at the command of the Spirit. So let us help them and make commemorations on their behalf. For if the sacrifices their father offered purified the sons of Job, why do you doubt that, when we too offer on behalf of those who have departed, some consolation comes to them? For God is accustomed

to grant favours to some on behalf of others. Paul shows this when he says, 'so that, from many persons, thanks may be given on our behalf for the gift granted to us through many.' So let us not grow weary of helping those who have departed, of offering on their behalf, and of entreating that prayers be made for them. For the common commemoration of the world, in which we trust, is set before us. That is why, with confidence, we make our requests on behalf of the world, and then we name them along with the martyrs, the confessors and the priests. For we are all one body, even though some members are more glorious than others. And we can gather forgiveness for them from every side: from prayers, from the offerings made on their behalf, and from those who are named along with them. Why, then, are you pained? Why do you mourn, when it is possible to gather so much forgiveness for the one who has departed [?]? From the sixty-second homily of the commentary on the Gospel of John: If the one who died was a sinner and greatly angered God, it is right to weep, or rather, not only to weep, for that would not help him at all. Let us instead do the things that can bring him some consolation: alms and offerings. The honour of the dead does not lie in wailing and lamentation

but in hymns and psalms and in living an orderly life. For the one who has departed is escorted by the angels, even if no one [escorts] the wretched and miserable corpse [?]. But if someone is impure, even if the whole city escorts him, he will not be lifted up. I want you to honour the one who has gone; honour him in another way, by giving alms for him. From the third homily of the commentary on the Letter to the Philippians: It was not in vain that the apostles laid down as a law that at the awesome mysteries there should be a commemoration of those who have departed. For we know that great benefit comes to them, and no small benefit. When the whole people stands with hands outstretched, and the whole priestly body is there, and the awesome divine sacrifice lies before them, how could we fail to persuade God when we make supplication for them? But this is for those who have departed in faith. Catechumens are not counted worthy even of this consolation; they are deprived of all this help, except for one thing. What is that? That it is possible to give to the poor on their behalf, for this brings some consolation. For God wills that we should benefit one another. Otherwise why, for the peace

and stability of the world, did he command us to pray? Why for all people? Look, among them all there are robbers, grave-robbers, thieves, and people full of many evils. Yet we pray for everyone, that they may come to repentance. So just as we pray for the living, who in no way differ from the dead, so we can also pray for the dead. Again, Judas Maccabeus and the children of Israel who were with him were fighting against the Idumeans. Those of Judas's house prepared themselves and came to Judas after a day and said to him, 'Let them take the bodies of those who fell and bury them in the tombs of their fathers.' And as they were burying them they found that under the clothing of each of them gold was hidden, taken from idols that were among those which the law commanded them not to approach. This became known to all and was believed by all: that this was why the soldiers had fallen. They all blessed God for his just judgement, who [?] the things the dead had hidden and showed them openly. And they began to pray and to ask God

that because of this the sin might not be fully reckoned against them. Judas laid on the whole people a levy of money, collected three thousand pieces of silver, and sent them to Jerusalem so that sacrifices might be offered on their behalf. He did this justly and rightly, because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead. For if he had not hoped for and awaited the resurrection of the dead, it would have been foolish and contemptible for anyone to pray for the dead and to offer sacrifices. For he was looking and waiting
Here ends the Book of the Soul, composed by Moses bar Kepha.
It is completed according to the strength that our Lord Jesus gave. Glory to his name for ever.

Others, then, performed temporal triumphs as a reward, and vain men were thought worthy to be remembered for what they had done, so that they would be recalled in many later generations. Again, when they speak [?] … those who were made and accomplished by them, so that they may be brought to good remembrance before the Creator. And they set names on engraved stones and monasteries [?], and arranged them in [?], by the order and the strength that completes [?]. But in works far from what is fitting, the disciple of Rabban [?] the God-loving [?], Rabban Yosa [?], was stripped of good remembrance, and of the scant requests of rabbans who are sharp of insight and very [?]. They, in the brevity [?] of the arrangement of these pairs [?], were heeded because of my guilt [?], so as to meet the wishes of those who will examine these lines that I have written. Therefore, since I was confident that I should take such care as my wretchedness allows [?], I trust with all the greater hope that this will be of great benefit to me, and that I may escape the troubles, mishaps and toil that befall my humility in these smoky [?] dwellings. This I hope for through the help and supplication of the [?] and the prayers of discerning, God-loving and watchful men. In return for the labour and understanding with which I applied myself [?], may I be found worthy of freedom from the wiles of the Adversary and from his assaults that rush upon us [?] … [?]. May I be seen washed clean of whirling [?] speech, of the defilements and lawless deeds that I committed willfully [?], and set free from cunning [?], through the supplication of those who keep his [?] and of those who ask [?] his sign [?].

But if you examine this, O discerning and learned reader, and find words that are not right, or faults, or are offended by them, correct them as far as the understanding within you allows, but do not let your heart be angry with me. Make room for excuse and [?] the apostolic word, and pardon my lack of learning, for I have been renewed [?] in the rush of ignorance and the haste of dullness. But remember the love that is the bond of perfection, and remember me, the sinner, with a word that will profit me, so that I may find mercy at that inescapable judgment [?] of the lost. And when you bring me to good remembrance, you too will find mercy and receive a double reward when you speak a word of mercy from your mouth for me, and also for those who took care of me, and for my fathers in body and in spirit. Remember the word of the Apostle, or rather the commandment, which says: “Pray earnestly for one another, so that you may be healed.”

It was set down on Sunday, the eighth day of the first Teshri, in the year one thousand five hundred and forty-six, in the northern monastery of Mar Bar Sawma, which is near Qurias [?] [?], and in its [?], in the land of [?], fortified by God.
